spec.theme: A Central Asian conqueror's view of Hindustan after 1526

sources.context: Babur, a ruler from Central Asia, defeated the Sultan of Delhi at Panipat in 1526 and began Mughal rule in northern India; he wrote his memoirs in Chagatai Turkic.

items.stem: Babur's remarks about Hindustan's "masses of gold and silver" and "unnumbered and endless workmen" help explain which of the following about how Mughal rulers sustained their state?

options.text: They funded the state by taxing a large and productive population of farmers and artisans.
options.label: key
options.why: Babur values India for its wealth and huge labor force. Mughal rulers, especially from Akbar onward, paid for their state and army mainly with land revenue and taxes on a dense agrarian and artisan population, collected through officials and zamindars.

options.text: They paid their armies mainly with plunder seized from Central Asian cities such as Samarkand and Bukhara.
options.label: reversal
options.why: This turns the situation around. Babur had lost his Central Asian lands to the Uzbeks, and India's wealth, not Central Asian loot, paid for Mughal power.

options.text: They depended chiefly on customs payments collected from European trading companies that controlled the major Indian ports.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: European companies did not control major Indian ports or provinces until the mid-eighteenth century and after, long after the Mughal revenue system took shape.

options.text: They drew most of their revenue from silver mines that the state operated directly across northern India.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Babur says nothing about mines. Northern India had little silver mining, and much of its silver came in through trade, so the Mughal fisc rested on land revenue, not state mines.

facts: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi, Sultan of Delhi, at Panipat in 1526.
Under Akbar (r. 1556-1605), the Mughal state paid for itself mainly through land revenue taken from the agrarian population, collected with the help of zamindars and officials.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Babur picks out India's gold and silver and its countless workmen as its main advantages, which points to the population and wealth that Mughal taxation relied on.
design.evidence_quote: it is a large country and has masses of gold and silver

items.stem: Babur's list of things missing in Hindustan, such as grapes, ice, hot baths, and colleges, most clearly reveals his point of view as

options.text: a Portuguese merchant evaluating the coastal markets of India for the Estado da India
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The excerpt is a Turkic-language memoir by a Central Asian conqueror. It says nothing about coastal trade or Portuguese interests.

options.text: a Timurid prince measuring India against the urban culture of Central Asia
options.label: key
options.why: The context line calls Babur a ruler from Central Asia who wrote in Chagatai Turkic. The fruits, cold water, bathhouses and colleges he misses are features of the Central Asian Timurid city life he grew up in.

options.text: a Sufi ascetic who rejected worldly comforts and urged rulers to renounce material wealth
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Babur complains about missing comforts and praises India's gold and silver, the opposite of an ascetic rejection of material things.

options.text: a Safavid envoy reporting to the shah in Tabriz about weaknesses in the new Mughal state
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The credit line names Babur himself, the founder of the Mughal dynasty, as the author. He was not a Safavid envoy.

facts: Babur was a descendant of Timur, was born in the Fergana Valley in 1483, and ruled from Kabul before invading India.
Babur wrote his memoirs in Chagatai Turkic.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The specific items Babur says he misses (grapes, musk-melons, ice, hot-baths, colleges) reflect a Central Asian outsider's standards, and the context line confirms his origin.
design.evidence_quote: no grapes, musk-melons or first-rate fruits, no ice or cold water

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would most directly challenge Babur's claim that Indian handicraft had no "form or symmetry, method or quality"?

options.text: Babur's army won at Panipat partly because it used matchlock firearms and field cannon.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This explains why Babur won, but the weapons were his own army's. It says nothing about Indian craftsmanship.

options.text: The Portuguese captured Goa in 1510 and forced Asian ships to buy passes called cartazes.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: This is true, but it concerns Portuguese naval power on the coast, not the quality of goods made by Indian artisans.

options.text: Indian cotton textiles were in high demand in markets across the Indian Ocean.
options.label: key
options.why: Indian cotton cloth was one of the most sought-after manufactured goods in Afro-Eurasian trade, and that demand undercuts Babur's dismissal of Indian craftsmanship.

options.text: Merchants shipped large amounts of pepper from the Malabar coast to ports in the Red Sea and Persian Gulf.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Pepper was a major Indian export, but it is a crop, not a handicraft, so it does not speak to Babur's claim about the quality of Indian work.

facts: Indian cotton textiles were among the most widely traded manufactured goods in the Indian Ocean world in the 1500s and 1600s.
The Portuguese captured Goa in 1510.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Babur's sweeping negative claim about Indian handicraft can be tested against the well-known reputation and trade of Indian cotton textiles.
design.evidence_quote: in handicraft and work there is no form or symmetry, method or quality

items.stem: Babur's conquest of northern India after the Battle of Panipat, described in the context line, is best understood as part of which broader development?

options.text: European trading companies seized territory in South Asia and ruled through local princes
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: European territorial rule in India began in the mid-eighteenth century, after Mughal power had declined, and it was not the setting for Babur's conquest.

options.text: Anticolonial movements mobilized peasants and elites to expel foreign conquerors from their lands
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Anticolonial nationalism belongs to the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Babur was a conqueror, not someone resisting foreign rule.

options.text: Mongol khanates united Eurasian trade routes under the heirs of Chinggis Khan
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Babur claimed descent from Chinggis Khan, but the Mongol khanates that unified Eurasian routes belonged to the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, not the 1520s.

options.text: Land-based empires used gunpowder weapons to expand and centralize their rule
options.label: key
options.why: Babur used firearms and artillery at Panipat in 1526. Like the Ottomans and Safavids in the same era, the Mughals relied on gunpowder weapons to build and hold a large land empire.

facts: Babur used firearms and field artillery in defeating Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526.
In the same era the Ottoman and Safavid empires also used gunpowder weapons to expand, as at the Ottoman victory over the Safavids at Chaldiran in 1514.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line says Babur defeated the Sultan of Delhi at Panipat in 1526 and began Mughal rule, which places the source within the expansion of the gunpowder land empires.

items.stem: EXTRA. Which of the following most limits the usefulness of the excerpt as evidence about society in Hindustan in the 1520s?

options.text: It records a newly arrived conqueror judging India by his homeland's tastes.
options.label: key
options.why: Babur wrote soon after conquering India and judged it by what he was used to in Central Asia, such as melons, ice and baths. His sweeping negatives tell us more about his own tastes than about Indian society.

options.text: It was intended to persuade the Delhi Sultan to surrender before the Battle of Panipat began.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt describes Hindustan after the victory, so it cannot have been addressed to the Sultan before the battle.

options.text: It was composed in Persian to flatter Hindu nobles whose support Babur needed to rule.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The context line says Babur wrote in Chagatai Turkic, and the excerpt criticizes India harshly instead of flattering its people.

options.text: It was written decades after Babur's death, when Mughal rule was already secure under Akbar.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The credit line dates the text to about 1526-1530, within Babur's lifetime. He died in 1530, and Akbar did not rule until 1556.

facts: Babur died in 1530.
Akbar ruled the Mughal Empire from 1556 to 1605.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The sweeping list of absences (no good looks, no manners, no genius) shows that an outsider's cultural standards shape the account, and the date and context line confirm he had only just arrived.
design.evidence_quote: Hindūstān is a country of few charms.

items.stem: EXTRA. Babur's situation as a Central Asian Muslim conqueror ruling a largely Hindu population was most similar to that of which of the following rulers?

options.text: Tokugawa shoguns governing Japan through daimyo drawn from the same warrior class
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Tokugawa were Japanese rulers governing a Japanese population, so they were not a foreign elite ruling a different majority.

options.text: Manchu emperors of the Qing ruling a mostly Han Chinese population
options.label: key
options.why: Like the Mughals, the Qing were a conquering dynasty from outside the core land, and they ruled a majority population that differed from them in ethnicity and culture.

options.text: Safavid shahs who made Twelver Shia Islam the official faith of their Persian empire
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Safavids did impose Shia Islam, but they brought their subjects into the rulers' faith. They did not rule a large majority of a different religion, as the Mughals did.

options.text: Ming emperors who restored Han Chinese rule after driving out the Mongol Yuan
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Ming were a native dynasty that replaced foreign conquerors, the opposite of Babur's position as an outside conqueror.

facts: The Manchu Qing dynasty conquered Beijing in 1644 and ruled a mostly Han Chinese population.
The Ming dynasty, founded in 1368, replaced the Mongol Yuan.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line identifies Babur as a ruler from Central Asia who took power in northern India, and that outsider-conqueror position is the basis for the comparison.

spec.theme: Akbar's religious discussions and Mughal rule

sources.context: A British army officer and historian wrote this book about the Mughal emperor Akbar, who ruled from 1556 to 1605, for a series on the rulers of India.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the main claim Malleson makes about the Thursday discussions at Fatehpur-Sikri?

options.text: Akbar banned all Muslim officials from state office after they showed rudeness in the Ibadat-Khana debates
options.label: overstated
options.why: Akbar only warned that anyone who offended again would have to leave the hall. The excerpt says nothing about removing anyone from office.

options.text: Abulfazl dominated the debates from the start and drove the leading Muslim scholars out of the hall
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt says Abulfazl at first took only a subordinate part, pushing the scholars to answer one another.

options.text: Akbar grew disillusioned with Muslim scholars whose debates revealed division and intolerance
options.label: key
options.why: Malleson says the scholars' bigotry and charges of infidelity against each other quite disgusted Akbar, who found many divisions instead of unity.

options.text: Akbar used the Thursday debates to unite Muslim scholars behind a common policy of persecuting Hindu subjects
options.label: reversal
options.why: The scholars agreed on persecuting Hindus, but the excerpt says this attitude disgusted Akbar. It did not become his policy.

facts: Akbar had the Ibadat-Khana (House of Worship) built at Fatehpur-Sikri in 1575 for religious discussions.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The passage stresses the scholars' bigotry, their divisions and their rudeness, and it says all of this disgusted Akbar.
design.evidence_quote: Instead of 'unity' in the creed of Islam he found a multiplicity of divisions.

items.stem: Which of the following developments would best support Malleson's argument that Akbar turned away from the views of the Muslim scholars at his court?

options.text: Aurangzeb reimposed the jizya on non-Muslims in 1679 and favored strict Sunni legal scholars at court
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This happened under a later emperor and points in the opposite direction, so it says nothing about Akbar's reaction to the debates.

options.text: The Ottoman sultans appointed a chief mufti, the Sheikh ul-Islam, to oversee religious law across the empire
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: This describes Ottoman religious administration, not Mughal India or Akbar's views.

options.text: Akbar's armies conquered Gujarat and Bengal in the 1570s, extending Mughal control to rich coastal provinces
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: These conquests are real, but they concern territorial expansion, not Akbar's attitude toward religious scholars.

options.text: Akbar later invited Hindu, Jain, Zoroastrian, and Christian scholars to the debates
options.label: key
options.why: Akbar opened the Ibadat-Khana debates to scholars of other faiths, including Jesuits from Goa in 1580. This shows him seeking answers beyond the quarreling Muslim scholars.

facts: Akbar opened the Ibadat-Khana discussions to Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians and Christians in the late 1570s.
Jesuit missionaries from Goa arrived at Akbar's court in 1580.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Malleson argues that the Muslim scholars' quarrels disgusted Akbar. His later invitation to other faiths would support that argument.
design.evidence_quote: quite disgusted Akbar

items.stem: The religious debates described in the excerpt took place within which of the following broader historical contexts?

options.text: A Muslim dynasty governing a population that was largely Hindu
options.label: key
options.why: The Mughals were Muslim rulers of a mostly Hindu South Asia. That is why it mattered so much whether scholars thought Hindus should be persecuted.

options.text: Renewed Mongol invasions that forced the Mughals to seek support from Central Asian clerics
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Mongol invasions of the 1200s were long over by Akbar's reign, and the excerpt does not mention outside invasion.

options.text: British East India Company officials pressuring Mughal emperors to accept missionaries
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Company did not gain political power in India until the mid-1700s, long after Akbar's reign.

options.text: A Mughal state newly converted to Shia Islam by order of its founding emperor
options.label: misattributed
options.why: This confuses the Mughals with the Safavids, whose ruler Ismail I made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion of Iran.

facts: The Mughal dynasty was Muslim, while most of its subjects in South Asia were Hindu.
The Safavid ruler Ismail I made Twelver Shia Islam Iran's official religion after 1501.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The scholars agreed it was right to persecute Hindus and other unbelievers, which shows the court was dealing with a large non-Muslim population.
design.evidence_quote: agreeing that it was right to persecute Hindus and other unbelievers

items.stem: Akbar's dissatisfaction with the attitudes described in the excerpt is most consistent with which of his policies toward non-Muslim subjects?

options.text: Organizing non-Muslims into self-governing millets led by their own religious authorities
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The millet system belonged to the Ottoman Empire, not the Mughal Empire.

options.text: Ending the jizya and recruiting Hindu Rajput nobles into imperial service
options.label: key
options.why: Akbar abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims and brought Rajput nobles into the mansabdar system. Both policies rejected the scholars' call to persecute Hindus.

options.text: Banning the construction of new Hindu temples and destroying temples in Varanasi and Mathura
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: These temple destructions happened under Aurangzeb in the later 1600s, not under Akbar.

options.text: Requiring Hindu officials to convert to Islam before receiving mansabdar ranks and land revenue grants
options.label: reversal
options.why: Akbar gave ranks to Hindu nobles without requiring conversion. Forced conversion would match the scholars' views, not his.

facts: Akbar abolished the jizya on non-Muslims in 1564.
Akbar brought Rajput nobles into Mughal service through alliances and marriage, beginning in 1562.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Akbar's disgust at scholars who favored persecuting Hindus fits his tolerant policies toward Hindu subjects.
design.evidence_quote: agreeing that it was right to persecute Hindus and other unbelievers, hurled charges of infidelity against each other

items.stem: Malleson's background, as described in the credit line, may limit the usefulness of the excerpt as evidence about Akbar's court mainly because Malleson

options.text: relied only on Hindu sources that were hostile to all Mughal rulers and their policies
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the credit line or excerpt identifies Malleson's sources. The passage actually names Abulfazl, who served at Akbar's court.

options.text: wrote in Persian for a Mughal court audience seeking to praise Akbar's ancestors
options.label: misattributed
options.why: This describes a court historian like Abulfazl, not a British officer writing for the Rulers of India series.

options.text: judged Mughal-era Muslim scholars through Victorian British assumptions
options.label: key
options.why: Malleson was a British officer writing in 1890, under British rule in India. Loaded words like bigotry and sectaries reflect his own era's views of Muslim religious leaders.

options.text: witnessed the Ibadat-Khana debates only briefly before Akbar closed the hall
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Malleson wrote in 1890, about three centuries after the debates, so he could not have seen them.

facts: Britain ruled India directly as the British Raj from 1858.
Akbar reigned from 1556 to 1605.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The credit line identifies the author as a British army officer writing in 1890, and the excerpt uses loaded words like bigotry and sectaries.
design.evidence_quote: The bigotry, the narrowness, evinced by the leaders of these sectaries

items.stem: Akbar's sponsorship of the religious discussions described in the excerpt was most similar to which of the following developments in another land-based empire?

options.text: Spanish monarchs expelling Jews in 1492 to enforce Catholic unity across their realms
options.label: reversal
options.why: Expelling a religious minority to force uniformity is the opposite of Akbar's tolerance.

options.text: The Ottoman devshirme converting Christian boys from the Balkans to serve as janissaries
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The devshirme was a way of recruiting soldiers and officials, not a ruler's patronage of debate between faiths.

options.text: Safavid shah Ismail I imposing Twelver Shia Islam as the official faith of Iran
options.label: reversal
options.why: Ismail enforced a single religious orthodoxy. That is the opposite of Akbar's open inquiry across faiths.

options.text: Qing emperor Kangxi hosting Jesuit scholars at his court in Beijing
options.label: key
options.why: Like Akbar, Kangxi welcomed scholars of a foreign faith to his court and issued an edict of toleration for Christianity in 1692.

facts: The Kangxi emperor employed Jesuits at the Qing court and issued an edict of toleration for Christianity in 1692.
Ferdinand and Isabella expelled Jews from Spain in 1492.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt describes a building put up specifically for regular religious discussions sponsored by the emperor.
design.evidence_quote: a building at Fatehpur-Sikri, erected for the purpose

spec.theme: Spanish colonization of the Caribbean and criticism of it

sources.context: Las Casas was a Spanish priest who took part in the Spanish settlement of the Caribbean and later argued for reform of Spanish treatment of Native peoples.

items.stem: Las Casas's purpose of persuading Spanish authorities to reform colonial practices most likely limits the usefulness of the excerpt as a source for which of the following?

options.text: Precise figures for the Native population of Hispaniola before 1492
options.label: key
options.why: Las Casas wanted to show how terrible the destruction was, so he had a reason to use dramatic numbers like 'Three Millions.' Historians dispute his figures, so the excerpt is weak evidence for exact population sizes.

options.text: The ways sixteenth-century reformers used vivid imagery to try to move royal officials
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The images of 'Tygers, Wolves and Lions' are good evidence of persuasive technique. Because his purpose was to persuade, that rhetoric is what the source shows best.

options.text: The attitudes of some Spanish missionaries toward the treatment of Native Caribbean peoples
options.label: reversal
options.why: A Dominican friar's own account directly shows one missionary's attitude, so his purpose does not limit it here.

options.text: Debates among Spanish clergy over whether the conquest of the Americas was morally legitimate
options.label: reversal
options.why: The source is a strong example of a clergyman condemning the conquest, so his reform purpose makes it more useful for this topic, not less.

facts: Las Casas wrote the Brief Account to push the Spanish Crown toward reform; it was published in 1552.
Historians dispute Las Casas's estimates of how many Native people lived in Hispaniola before contact.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt's dramatic count of three million people reduced to three hundred serves a reform argument, which makes it unreliable as an exact statistic.
design.evidence_quote: of Three Millions of Persons, which lived in Hispaniola itself

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would most directly modify the excerpt's explanation for the decline of the Native population of Hispaniola?

options.text: Royal decrees such as the New Laws of 1542 that restricted the inheritance of encomiendas
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The New Laws were a real response to abuses, but they say nothing about what caused the population decline.

options.text: Accounts showing that smallpox epidemics killed many Taino after 1518
options.label: key
options.why: Las Casas blames the decline on Spanish massacre and torture. Evidence that epidemic disease from the Columbian Exchange killed large numbers of people adds a major cause he leaves out, so it modifies his explanation.

options.text: Evidence that Columbus brought sugarcane and horses to Hispaniola on his second voyage
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: This is a real part of the Columbian Exchange, but it does not explain why the Native population fell.

options.text: Reports that encomenderos forced Taino laborers into gold mining with very little food
options.label: reversal
options.why: This evidence would support his argument that Spanish cruelty destroyed the population, not modify it.

facts: Smallpox reached Hispaniola around 1518 and caused heavy Taino deaths.
Old World diseases were the leading cause of Native population collapse in the Americas after 1492.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Las Casas puts the decline down entirely to Spanish massacre and torment, so evidence that disease played a major role would modify his claim.
design.evidence_quote: the Massacre of these Wretches, whom they have so inhumanely and barbarously butcher'd

items.stem: Which of the following describes a historical context in which the Spanish treatment of Caribbean peoples described in the excerpt took place?

options.text: English joint-stock companies founded sugar colonies on Barbados and Jamaica using enslaved Africans
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: English Caribbean colonies came in the seventeenth century (Barbados in the 1620s, Jamaica in 1655), well after the early Spanish settlement described here.

options.text: Portuguese traders set up coastal posts to buy gold and enslaved Africans in West Africa
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Portuguese posts in West Africa were real, but they are not the setting for Spanish treatment of Caribbean peoples.

options.text: Spanish settlers received grants of Native labor through the encomienda
options.label: key
options.why: In the early Caribbean colonies, the Crown granted Spanish settlers the right to Native labor and tribute through the encomienda. Las Casas himself was a former encomendero, and abuse under this system is central to his criticism.

options.text: Spanish officials relied on the mita labor draft to staff the silver mines of Potosi in the Andes
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Spanish adapted the mita for Potosi in the Andes from the 1570s, which is a different region and a later time than the early Caribbean settlement described here.

facts: The Spanish Crown granted encomiendas in the Caribbean starting in the early 1500s, giving settlers rights to Native labor and tribute.
Las Casas held an encomienda before he gave it up and became a critic of the system.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The credit line calls Las Casas a former encomendero, and the excerpt describes forty years of Spanish rule over Native peoples after the first landing.
design.evidence_quote: studying nothing, for the space of Forty Years, after their first landing

items.stem: The depopulation of Caribbean islands described in the excerpt most directly contributed to which of the following developments in the sixteenth-century Caribbean?

options.text: The abolition of the encomienda system across all of Spanish America by royal decree in 1542
options.label: overstated
options.why: The New Laws of 1542 limited encomiendas, for example by restricting inheritance, but did not abolish them, and colonists resisted them.

options.text: A shift by Spanish colonists toward growing cotton for export to English textile factories
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: English factory textile production belongs to the Industrial Revolution of the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, not the sixteenth century.

options.text: The rise of a large mestizo elite that took control of Caribbean colonial governments
options.label: overstated
options.why: Mestizo populations did grow, but peninsulares appointed from Spain controlled colonial government, and mestizos ranked below them in the casta hierarchy.

options.text: Spanish colonists' growing use of enslaved Africans as laborers
options.label: key
options.why: As the Native population collapsed, Spanish colonists in Hispaniola and nearby islands turned to enslaved Africans to work on sugar estates and in mines, which helped grow the Atlantic slave trade.

facts: Spanish colonists began bringing enslaved Africans to Hispaniola in the early 1500s as Native labor declined.
The New Laws of 1542 restricted but did not end the encomienda system.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt describes islands left 'unpeopled and desolate,' which means a labor shortage that colonists filled with enslaved Africans.
design.evidence_quote: unpeopled and desolate

items.stem: Las Casas's description of Native Caribbean peoples as 'innocent Sheep' most likely reflects which of the following?

options.text: His view as a friar that Native peoples were souls needing protection
options.label: key
options.why: As a Dominican friar, Las Casas saw Native peoples as innocent souls who could become Christians and deserved the Crown's protection. The image of sheep, which in Christian language need a protecting shepherd, fits this view.

options.text: His goal as a royal official of expanding Spanish gold mining across the conquered islands
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The excerpt condemns the destruction caused by Spanish exploitation. It does not promote more mining.

options.text: His support for Protestant critics of the Catholic Church in kingdoms that were Spain's rivals
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Las Casas was a Catholic friar. Protestant rivals later used his work against Spain, but he did not support them.

options.text: His belief, shared with Sepulveda, that Native peoples were natural slaves suited to forced labor
options.label: reversal
options.why: At the Valladolid debate (1550 to 1551), Sepulveda argued the natural-slave position and Las Casas argued against it.

facts: Las Casas was a Dominican friar who argued that Native peoples were rational beings who could be converted to Christianity.
At the Valladolid debate of 1550 to 1551, Las Casas opposed Juan Gines de Sepulveda's argument that Native peoples were natural slaves.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The sheep image together with the credit line's 'Dominican friar' shows a religious view of Native peoples as innocents to be protected.
design.evidence_quote: assaulted the innocent Sheep

items.stem: The translation of Las Casas's account into English in 1583, as noted in the credit line, is best understood in the context of which broader development?

options.text: The Catholic Reformation's campaign to spread the Jesuit order across Protestant northern Europe
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Jesuit missions were a Catholic effort, and they do not explain why Protestant England would publish an attack on Spanish colonial conduct.

options.text: Rivalry between Spain and Protestant states over trade and empire
options.label: key
options.why: In the late 1500s, England and the Dutch were competing with Catholic Spain for Atlantic trade and colonies. Accounts of Spanish cruelty, including this one, were circulated in their countries and fed anti-Spanish propaganda.

options.text: The Seven Years' War, during which Britain seized Spanish possessions in the Caribbean
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Seven Years' War (1756 to 1763) came almost two centuries after the 1583 translation.

options.text: Cooperation between Spain and England in suppressing the Atlantic slave trade by naval patrols
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: British naval patrols against the slave trade began after 1807, and in 1583 Spain and England were moving toward war, not working together.

facts: Anglo-Spanish rivalry grew in the 1580s and led to war, including the Spanish Armada of 1588.
Translations of Las Casas's account were used in Protestant countries to portray Spanish colonization as cruel.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The credit line says the first English translation came out in 1583, a time of growing English rivalry with Spain.

spec.theme: The Atlantic slave trade as experienced and recounted by a survivor

sources.context: Equiano was a formerly enslaved man living in London when he published this autobiography in 1789, during a British campaign to end the slave trade.

items.stem: Based on the context of its publication, Equiano's description of his arrival on the slave ship was most likely intended to

options.text: defend the traditional systems of slavery in Africa as a model for reforming plantation labor
options.label: overstated
options.why: The passage does compare the ship unfavorably with slavery in his homeland, but it never offers African practices as a model for reforming plantations.

options.text: encourage West African rulers to stop selling war captives to European traders on the coast
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The book was published in London for a British readership during a British abolition campaign. It was not addressed to African rulers.

options.text: persuade British readers that the slave trade was cruel and should be ended
options.label: key
options.why: The context line says the work was published in London in 1789 during a British campaign to end the slave trade. Vivid scenes of terror, chains and despair served that abolitionist purpose.

options.text: convince British merchants that slave ships needed larger crews and better supplies for long voyages
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the passage proposes improving how slave ships operated. The author was an abolitionist who wanted the trade ended, not reformed.

facts: The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano was published in London in 1789.
A British movement to abolish the slave trade was active in the late 1780s, and Parliament abolished the British slave trade in 1807.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line places publication in London in 1789 during a British campaign to end the slave trade, and the passage stresses the horror of the ship.
design.evidence_quote: quite overpowered with horror and anguish, I fell motionless on the deck and fainted

items.stem: Which of the following claims does Equiano make in the excerpt about his situation aboard the slave ship?

options.text: His captors were fellow Africans who spoke a language closely related to his own
options.label: reversal
options.why: He stresses that the crew's complexions, hair and language were completely unfamiliar to him.

options.text: He welcomed the voyage as an escape from the harsh slavery of his own country
options.label: reversal
options.why: He describes terror and despair, and he says he would have preferred even the lowest slave status at home.

options.text: The European crew planned to return him to the coast after examining his health
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The crew did check whether he was sound, but he concluded they meant to kill him. He never says they planned to return him.

options.text: It was worse than the condition of the lowest slave in his home society
options.label: key
options.why: He says he would have given up ten thousand worlds to trade places with the meanest slave in his own country, which means the ship was far worse than slavery as he knew it.

facts: In the 1700s, forms of slavery and dependent labor existed in many West African societies alongside the Atlantic trade.

design.key_evidence_in_source: His statement that he would have traded ten thousand worlds to have the condition of the meanest slave in his own country.
design.evidence_quote: exchanged my condition with that of the meanest slave in my own country

items.stem: The slave ship that Equiano describes as "waiting for its cargo" was part of a trade that expanded greatly in the 1600s and 1700s mainly because of

options.text: rising demand for labor on sugar and other cash-crop plantations in the Americas
options.label: key
options.why: Sugar plantations in Brazil and the Caribbean, and later tobacco, rice and cotton plantations, created a huge demand for enslaved African labor, so the Atlantic trade grew rapidly in the 1600s and 1700s.

options.text: Indigenous population decline that completely ended the use of Native American forced labor
options.label: overstated
options.why: Disease did reduce Indigenous populations and helped raise demand for African labor. But Indigenous forced labor, such as the mita in the Andes, continued.

options.text: the spread of industrial factories in Britain that required large numbers of unfree workers
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Industrialization mostly came after 1750, and British factories used wage labor, not enslaved Africans shipped across the Atlantic.

options.text: the Ottoman Empire's demand for soldiers recruited through the devshirme system in the Balkans
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The devshirme took Christian boys from the Balkans for Ottoman service. It had nothing to do with Atlantic shipments from the West African coast.

facts: Sugar plantations in Brazil and the Caribbean depended heavily on enslaved African labor in the 1600s and 1700s.
The volume of the Atlantic slave trade peaked in the 1700s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The ship riding at anchor and waiting for its cargo of captives points to the large-scale commercial trade that supplied labor to plantations in the Americas.
design.evidence_quote: a slave ship, which was then riding at anchor, and waiting for its cargo

items.stem: The trade in captives shown in the excerpt was most directly connected to which development in West Africa between 1450 and 1750?

options.text: The Songhai Empire expanded its control of trans-Saharan trade by banning sales of captives to Europeans
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Songhai fell to a Moroccan invasion in 1591, and it was never known for banning sales to Europeans. Coastal states, not Songhai, dominated the Atlantic trade.

options.text: Some states, such as Dahomey, grew by selling captives to Europeans for goods like guns
options.label: key
options.why: Coastal and inland states such as Dahomey and Asante grew stronger by supplying captives to European traders in exchange for firearms, textiles and other goods.

options.text: West African rulers adopted Christianity as a state religion to gain access to Portuguese trading posts
options.label: overstated
options.why: A few rulers, like those of Kongo in west-central Africa, did adopt Christianity, but most West African rulers did not make it a state religion.

options.text: European states conquered most of the West African interior and ruled it through direct colonial administration
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Before 1750, Europeans mostly stayed in coastal forts and trading posts. Conquest of the interior came in the late 1800s.

facts: The Kingdom of Dahomey expanded in the 1700s partly through the slave trade with Europeans.
European traders exchanged firearms, textiles and other manufactured goods for captives on the West African coast.
The Songhai Empire was defeated by a Moroccan army in 1591.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The ship arrives at the coast to collect captives, which reflects a trade in which African suppliers delivered people to European ships at the coast.
design.evidence_quote: when I arrived on the coast was the sea, and a slave ship

items.stem: Which of the following might limit a historian's use of the excerpt as evidence about the experience of captives at the start of the Middle Passage?

options.text: It describes only the trade in the Indian Ocean rather than voyages across the Atlantic
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt and its title deal with the Atlantic slave trade. Nothing in it refers to the Indian Ocean.

options.text: It was censored by Portuguese officials who controlled printing in eighteenth-century London
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the credit or context line suggests any censorship, and Portuguese officials did not control printing in London.

options.text: It was published decades later in a campaign to persuade readers against the trade
options.label: key
options.why: The context line places publication in 1789 during an abolition campaign, so the account was written to persuade. Historians have also debated parts of his account of his early life, so it should be read as a published abolitionist narrative.

options.text: It was written by a ship's captain who wanted to justify the conditions aboard his vessel
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The credit line identifies the author as a formerly enslaved man who became an abolitionist, not a ship's captain.

facts: Equiano's Interesting Narrative was published in 1789 as part of the British antislavery movement.
Historians have debated parts of Equiano's account of his African childhood because of records suggesting a birth in South Carolina.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line says the autobiography was published in 1789 by a formerly enslaved man during a British campaign to end the slave trade.

items.stem: Which of the following was an effect on West African societies of the trade in captives that Equiano describes?

options.text: Local textile production collapsed because of competition from British steam-powered mills
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Steam-powered textile mills came after 1750, during the Industrial Revolution, so they fall outside the period of this trade.

options.text: Islam disappeared from the region as coastal states converted to Christianity
options.label: overstated
options.why: Islam stayed strong in much of West Africa, especially the Sahel. Christian conversion was limited in this period.

options.text: Population grew sharply as American food crops replaced the export of captives
options.label: reversal
options.why: American crops such as maize and cassava did reach Africa, but the export of captives continued and grew. They did not replace it.

options.text: Gender imbalances developed because more men than women were taken
options.label: key
options.why: Plantation buyers preferred male laborers, so more men than women were shipped across the Atlantic. This left some West African societies with more women than men.

facts: More enslaved men than women were transported across the Atlantic, which contributed to gender imbalances in parts of West Africa.
Islam remained widespread in West Africa throughout the period 1450 to 1750.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The multitude of chained captives shows the large-scale removal of people from West Africa, which is the cause of the demographic effects described in the key.
design.evidence_quote: a multitude of black people of every description chained together

spec.theme: Industrial capitalism and the world market in the mid-19th century

sources.context: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels wrote this political program in 1847 and 1848 for a group of European socialists called the Communist League.

items.stem: The excerpt's reference to industries using "raw material drawn from the remotest zones" most directly reflects which nineteenth-century economic process?

options.text: British textile mills spinning raw cotton grown in the southern United States and India
options.label: key
options.why: British mechanized cotton spinning, the leading industry of the 1840s, depended on cotton imported from distant regions, mainly the slave plantations of the US South and also India. This is exactly the far-off raw material the excerpt describes.

options.text: Russian nobles expanding serf labor on their estates to grow grain mostly for local consumption
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Serf agriculture producing for local needs is the kind of local self-sufficiency the excerpt says is disappearing. It does not show industry drawing on raw material from distant zones.

options.text: Latin American states building tariff-protected factories to replace European imports right after independence
options.label: reversal
options.why: After independence in the 1820s, Latin American economies mostly exported raw materials and bought European manufactures. That is the reverse of local factory building, and it fits the excerpt's picture of dependence on foreign goods.

options.text: European trading companies such as the Dutch East India Company shipping spices from Southeast Asian islands
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The spice trade run by joint-stock companies peaked in the 1600s and 1700s. It dealt in luxury goods, not raw material for factory industry, and the Dutch East India Company was dissolved in 1799.

facts: In the first half of the 1800s, British cotton mills relied on imported raw cotton, mostly from the southern United States.
Cotton textiles were the leading sector of the British Industrial Revolution.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The passage describes new industries that process raw material from far away instead of local material, which matches British mills' dependence on imported cotton.
design.evidence_quote: industries that no longer work up indigenous raw material, but raw material drawn from the remotest zones

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the main claim of the excerpt?

options.text: National governments are using tariffs to shield traditional industries, which is slowing the growth of world trade
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt says the opposite. It claims old national industries are being destroyed every day and that 'Reactionists' cannot stop this.

options.text: The search for markets is replacing national self-sufficiency with global economic interdependence.
options.label: key
options.why: The passage argues that the bourgeoisie's need for ever-larger markets has broken down local and national self-sufficiency and made nations depend on one another.

options.text: Global trade is expanding mainly because European monarchs seek colonies for prestige and military power
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The excerpt says the expansion comes from the bourgeoisie's economic need for markets, not from the political goals of monarchs.

options.text: Workers of all countries must unite to overthrow the bourgeoisie through a violent seizure of state power
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Manifesto as a whole does call for proletarian revolution, but this passage only describes how the world market is built. It makes no call to action.

facts: The Manifesto of the Communist Party was published in 1848.
Marx and Engels argued that the bourgeoisie, the capitalist class, drove economic change.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The closing sentence sums up the argument: self-sufficiency is giving way to universal interdependence.
design.evidence_quote: In place of the old local and national seclusion and self-sufficiency, we have intercourse in every direction, universal inter-dependence of nations.

items.stem: Which of the following conditions in the 1840s provides the most direct context for the excerpt's description of the world market?

options.text: Russian revolutionaries had established a communist state that nationalized industry and banned private trade
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The first communist state came out of the 1917 Bolshevik Revolution, about seventy years after the excerpt.

options.text: Japan's Meiji government was building railroads and factories to compete with Western industrial powers
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Meiji Restoration began in 1868, and state-led industrialization came after that, so it could not have shaped a text from 1848.

options.text: Britain's early industrial lead had made it the chief exporter of factory-made goods
options.label: key
options.why: By the 1840s, Britain's mechanized industries, textiles above all, exported manufactured goods across the world. That is the global reach of production and consumption the authors were describing.

options.text: European states were dividing Africa among themselves under rules set at the Berlin Conference
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Berlin Conference took place in 1884 to 1885, decades after the Manifesto was written in 1847 and 1848.

facts: Britain was the first country to industrialize, beginning in the late 1700s.
By the mid-1800s Britain was the world's leading exporter of manufactured goods, especially cotton textiles.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The 1848 date in the credit line and the description of products consumed 'in every quarter of the globe' point to Britain-led industrial exports of the 1840s.
design.evidence_quote: industries whose products are consumed, not only at home, but in every quarter of the globe

items.stem: Which of the following was a nineteenth-century development outside Europe that resulted from the process the excerpt describes as destroying "old-established national industries"?

options.text: Japan's shogunate tightened its seclusion policy after American warships arrived in Edo Bay in 1853
options.label: reversal
options.why: After Perry's arrival, Japan signed the Treaty of Kanagawa in 1854 and opened its ports. Its seclusion ended rather than tightened.

options.text: Ming China's silk and porcelain exports drew large amounts of American silver into its economy
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The silver flow into Ming China belongs to the 1500s and 1600s, and it involved Chinese exports doing well, not local industry being destroyed.

options.text: The Qing kept all foreign trade confined to Canton under the cohong system through the end of the century
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Canton system ended with the Treaty of Nanjing in 1842, after the First Opium War. China was forced to open more ports, not to keep trade confined.

options.text: Hand-loom weaving in India declined as cheaper British machine-made cloth entered its markets
options.label: key
options.why: In the 1800s, imports of cheap British factory cloth undercut India's hand-loom weavers. This is a well-known case of an old industry destroyed by the world market.

facts: In the 1800s, imports of British machine-made cotton cloth contributed to the decline of India's hand-loom textile industry.
The Treaty of Nanjing (1842) ended the Canton system and opened additional Chinese ports to foreign trade.
The Treaty of Kanagawa (1854) began opening Japan to American trade after Perry's 1853 expedition.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt claims that national industries are being displaced by new industries whose products are sold worldwide, and Indian textiles are a standard example.
design.evidence_quote: All old-established national industries have been destroyed or are daily being destroyed.

items.stem: EXTRA. Based on the context line and the excerpt, the passage was most likely written in order to

options.text: explain capitalism's global reach to socialists building a political movement
options.label: key
options.why: The context line says this was a political program for the Communist League, a group of socialists. The passage analyzes the bourgeoisie's world market as background for the movement's program.

options.text: defend traditional guilds and national industries against competition from foreign producers
options.label: reversal
options.why: The authors note the 'chagrin of Reactionists' with some irony and treat the destruction of old industries as a historical fact, not something to resist.

options.text: advise factory owners on how to find new overseas markets for their manufactured goods
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the credit line or the text suggests an audience of businessmen. The bourgeoisie is described as a class being 'chased' by its own needs, not advised.

options.text: persuade European governments to follow Britain's 1846 repeal of the Corn Laws and adopt free trade
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Free-trade campaigns were run by liberals and merchants. The Manifesto was addressed to socialists, not governments, and it criticizes the bourgeoisie rather than promoting its policies.

facts: Marx and Engels wrote the Manifesto for the Communist League, published in 1848.
Britain repealed the Corn Laws in 1846.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line names the audience (the Communist League) and calls the document a political program, while the text mocks reactionaries' resistance to the change.
design.evidence_quote: To the great chagrin of Reactionists, it has drawn from under the feet of industry the national ground on which it stood.

items.stem: EXTRA. Which development later in the nineteenth century would most strengthen the excerpt's argument about the "universal inter-dependence of nations"?

options.text: The emancipation of Russian serfs in 1861, which freed peasants from legal ties to landowners
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Emancipation was a domestic reform in Russia. It does not show nations becoming dependent on one another through trade.

options.text: The opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 and the laying of undersea telegraph cables
options.label: key
options.why: The Suez Canal shortened sea routes between Europe and Asia, and undersea cables carried news and prices quickly between continents. Both tied distant markets more closely together, which supports the excerpt's claim.

options.text: The Taiping Rebellion's effort to create a new religious kingdom in southern and central China
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Taiping Rebellion (1850 to 1864) was an internal religious and political uprising. It is not evidence of growing global economic interdependence.

options.text: The adoption of high protective tariffs by Germany and the United States in the late 1800s
options.label: reversal
options.why: Protective tariffs, such as Germany's in 1879, shielded national industries. They would complicate the excerpt's claim rather than strengthen it.

facts: The Suez Canal opened in 1869.
A lasting transatlantic telegraph cable was completed in 1866.
Germany adopted protective tariffs in 1879.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt's claim of 'intercourse in every direction' would be supported by later transportation and communication links between continents.
design.evidence_quote: we have intercourse in every direction, universal inter-dependence of nations

spec.theme: Railways, telegraphs and imperial ambition in Africa

sources.context: Cecil Rhodes was a British businessman and politician in southern Africa who proposed a railway and telegraph line from Cape Town to Cairo; this cartoon was printed in a British magazine in 1892.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the historical situation in which this cartoon of Cecil Rhodes was published in 1892?

options.text: Abolition of the Atlantic slave trade had just ended all European commercial interest in the African interior
options.label: overstated
options.why: Britain abolished its slave trade in 1807, long before 1892. European commercial interest in the African interior rose sharply after that.

options.text: African kingdoms had expelled European merchants from most of their coastal trading forts in West Africa
options.label: reversal
options.why: In the 1890s European control in West Africa was growing, not shrinking.

options.text: European states were rapidly claiming African territory in the decade after the Berlin Conference.
options.label: key
options.why: The cartoon came out in 1892, during the Scramble for Africa that sped up after the Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885. It shows a British figure claiming the continent from south to north.

options.text: Britain was pulling back from Africa after suffering costly defeats in the South African War against the Boer republics
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The South African War was fought from 1899 to 1902, after the cartoon was made. Britain also did not withdraw from Africa after it.

facts: The Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885 set rules for European claims to African territory.
Britain abolished its slave trade in 1807.
The South African (Anglo-Boer) War was fought from 1899 to 1902.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The credit line dates the cartoon to 1892, and the image shows a British figure standing over the whole African map.
design.evidence_quote: Striding from Cape Town to Cairo

items.stem: The cartoonist's depiction of Rhodes as a giant standing astride the map of Africa most directly conveys which claim?

options.text: The telegraph line would mainly benefit African farmers by linking them to new overseas markets
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: No African farmers or markets appear in the image. The cartoon is about Rhodes's ambition, not who would benefit.

options.text: France and Germany had already secured control of the land between Cape Town and Cairo
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: No rival powers appear in the cartoon. It presents the land as open to Rhodes's stride.

options.text: African states were powerful enough to keep British railway and telegraph builders confined to the coasts
options.label: reversal
options.why: The cartoon shows Rhodes spanning the interior. Nothing in it suggests that British builders were held back to the coasts.

options.text: Rhodes's ambitions aimed at a British presence stretching across the whole continent
options.label: key
options.why: One boot is at the southern tip and the other far to the north, and he holds a wire across Africa. Together these show ambition that covers the whole continent from Cape Town to Cairo.

facts: Cecil Rhodes promoted a Cape-to-Cairo railway and telegraph line in the 1890s.
Rhodes served as prime minister of the Cape Colony from 1890 to 1896.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The giant's boots are placed at the southern and northern ends of Africa, and the caption names Cape Town and Cairo.
design.evidence_quote: The Rhodes Colossus: Striding from Cape Town to Cairo

items.stem: The telegraph wire Rhodes holds in the cartoon is best understood as part of which broader process of the nineteenth century?

options.text: Industrial technologies helped European states extend and coordinate control over distant colonies
options.label: key
options.why: Telegraphs, railways and steamships were industrial technologies that let imperial powers send orders, troops and goods quickly. Rhodes's proposed line fits this pattern.

options.text: The Columbian Exchange carried new crops and diseases between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Columbian Exchange began after 1492 and has no link to telegraph technology.

options.text: Islamic reform movements such as the Sokoto Caliphate spread through jihad across the West African savanna
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Sokoto Caliphate was a real development of the 1800s, but it was an African religious and political movement that had nothing to do with British telegraph building.

options.text: The spread of Enlightenment ideas through printed pamphlets encouraged colonial independence movements across the Americas
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: That process belongs to the late 1700s and early 1800s. It is not connected to a telegraph serving imperial expansion in Africa.

facts: Electric telegraph networks spread worldwide in the second half of the 1800s, including undersea cables.
Railways and telegraphs helped European states govern and exploit colonies in the late 1800s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Rhodes holds a telegraph wire that runs across Africa, and the context line notes his proposed railway and telegraph line.
design.evidence_quote: proposed a railway and telegraph line from Cape Town to Cairo

items.stem: Which of the following projects was most similar to the Cape-to-Cairo plan associated with Rhodes in the cartoon?

options.text: The Tokugawa shogunate's restriction of foreign merchants to a single Dutch trading post at Nagasaki
options.label: reversal
options.why: This was a pre-1750 policy that limited outside contact. It was not a project to expand an empire's reach.

options.text: Russia's Trans-Siberian Railway, begun in 1891 to link European Russia with the Pacific coast
options.label: key
options.why: Like the Cape-to-Cairo plan, the Trans-Siberian Railway was an industrial-age transport project meant to tie together a huge empire across a continent.

options.text: The Inca road network, whose relay runners carried messages and tribute records along the length of the Andes
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Inca roads did connect an empire, but they came centuries earlier and did not use industrial technology.

options.text: The Ming dynasty's rebuilding of the Great Wall to defend its northern frontier against Mongol raids
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This was a defensive building project from before 1750. It did not use industrial technology to tie an empire together.

facts: Construction of the Trans-Siberian Railway began in 1891.
The Inca road system was built before Spanish conquest in the 1530s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The caption and the context line identify a railway and telegraph plan spanning a continent, which students compare with another empire's continental railway.
design.evidence_quote: proposed a railway and telegraph line from Cape Town to Cairo

items.stem: EXTRA: The expansion of Rhodes's British South Africa Company into lands north of the Limpopo River most directly led to which development in the 1890s?

options.text: The Maji Maji rebellion against forced cotton growing in German East Africa
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Maji Maji took place from 1905 to 1907 and was aimed at German, not British, rule.

options.text: The Zulu kingdom's defeat of a British army column at the Battle of Isandlwana
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Isandlwana was fought in 1879 in Zululand. It came before the company's expansion and was not a result of it.

options.text: Armed risings by Ndebele and Shona peoples against company rule
options.label: key
options.why: The company occupied Mashonaland in 1890 and Matabeleland in 1893. Ndebele and Shona risings followed in 1896 to 1897.

options.text: Ethiopia's defeat of an invading Italian army at the Battle of Adwa in 1896
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Adwa happened in the 1890s, but it was resistance to Italy in northeast Africa and was not caused by Rhodes's company.

facts: The British South Africa Company was chartered in 1889 under Rhodes's leadership.
Ndebele and Shona risings against company rule took place in 1896 to 1897.
Ethiopia defeated Italy at Adwa in 1896.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line identifies Rhodes as a businessman and politician in southern Africa, and the cartoon shows him striding north from the Cape.
design.evidence_quote: British businessman and politician in southern Africa

items.stem: EXTRA: Which of the following is a limitation of this cartoon for historians studying the effects of British expansion on Africa?

options.text: It was published in an African newspaper, so it cannot show how British readers viewed Rhodes
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The context line says it was printed in a British magazine.

options.text: It shows the railway as completed, so it exaggerates how much British track was actually laid across Africa by 1892
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: No finished railway appears in the image. The caption shows Rhodes striding toward his goal, not a completed line.

options.text: It was drawn decades after Rhodes's death, so it cannot reflect views held during his career
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The credit line dates it to 1892, during Rhodes's active career.

options.text: It shows no Africans, so it reveals little about how colonized peoples experienced expansion
options.label: key
options.why: The cartoon shows only Rhodes over an empty map of Africa. It came from a British magazine for British readers, so it gives little evidence of African experiences or responses.

facts: Punch was a British humor magazine published in London.
The Cape-to-Cairo railway was never completed as a continuous line.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The image shows only the figure of Rhodes over the map of Africa, and the context line places its publication in a British magazine.
design.evidence_quote: this cartoon was printed in a British magazine in 1892

spec.theme: The 1915 deportations of Armenians in the Ottoman Empire

sources.context: Henry Morgenthau Sr. was the United States ambassador to the Ottoman Empire from 1913 to 1916; he published this book in 1918.

items.stem: Which of the following best explains how the historical situation in which Morgenthau published his account might limit its use as evidence about the deportations?

options.text: Published while the United States fought Germany, the book may reflect wartime hostility toward the Central Powers and their Ottoman ally.
options.label: key
options.why: The credit line dates the book to 1918, when the United States was at war with Germany (since April 1917), the Ottoman Empire's partner. A historian should weigh possible wartime bias, even though Morgenthau based his account on his own talks with Ottoman officials.

options.text: Because the United States had declared war on the Ottoman Empire in 1914, Morgenthau was barred from speaking with any Ottoman officials.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The United States never declared war on the Ottoman Empire, and the excerpt itself describes his conversations with Turkish authorities.

options.text: As an official writing for Ottoman officials, Morgenthau likely softened his description so as to protect continued American diplomatic access in Constantinople.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the source suggests an Ottoman audience, and the language is harsh rather than softened. He published in 1918, after he had left the post.

options.text: Because Morgenthau left his post in 1916, he could only have learned of the 1915 deportations years later through secondhand newspaper reports printed in New York.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The context line says he was ambassador from 1913 to 1916, so he was in office during the 1915 deportations, and the text cites his own conversations with Ottoman officials.

facts: The United States declared war on Germany in April 1917 and on Austria-Hungary in December 1917.
The United States never declared war on the Ottoman Empire, which entered World War I on the side of the Central Powers in 1914.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The credit line's 1918 publication date by a US ambassador puts the book in the period when the United States was at war with the Central Powers.
design.evidence_quote: in their conversations with me, they made no particular attempt to conceal the fact

items.stem: The deportations Morgenthau describes in the spring and summer of 1915 are best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.text: Mustafa Kemal's new Turkish Republic was carrying out population exchanges with Greece as part of the peace settlement ending the war.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Turkish Republic was founded in 1923, and the Greek-Turkish exchange followed the 1923 Lausanne settlement, several years after 1915.

options.text: Fighting Russia in World War I, Ottoman leaders treated Armenians as a potential internal threat along the empire's eastern front.
options.label: key
options.why: The 1915 deportations took place during the Ottoman war against Russia in the Caucasus. The Committee of Union and Progress government portrayed Armenians as disloyal and used wartime conditions to remove them.

options.text: Allied powers enforcing the Treaty of Sèvres were dividing Anatolia into zones and moving populations to separate rival ethnic groups.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Treaty of Sèvres was signed in 1920, after the war, and was never fully put into effect. It cannot explain events in 1915.

options.text: Ottoman reformers of the Tanzimat era were creating new legal categories that sorted subjects into separate religious communities for taxation.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Tanzimat reforms belong to the mid-nineteenth century. They also aimed at legal equality among subjects and did not involve deportation.

facts: The Ottoman Empire entered World War I in 1914 and fought Russia on the Caucasus front.
The Committee of Union and Progress government ordered mass deportations of Armenians in 1915.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt dates the deportations to spring and summer 1915, during the Ottoman Empire's World War I fighting.
design.evidence_quote: All through the spring and summer of 1915 the deportations took place.

items.stem: Based on the excerpt, the treatment of Armenians in 1915 was most similar to which later mass atrocity in the twentieth century?

options.text: Like the Amritsar massacre of 1919, it was a single violent episode in which colonial troops fired on unarmed protesters in one city.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt describes a months-long campaign across nearly every place Armenians lived, not one episode in one city.

options.text: Like the 1947 partition of India, it resulted mainly from a departing colonial power's hasty drawing of borders between religious communities.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The deportations were ordered by the Ottoman authorities themselves, as the excerpt states. No departing colonial power drew borders.

options.text: Like the Holocaust, it was a wartime effort by a state to destroy an entire people defined by ethnicity or religion rather than by class.
options.label: key
options.why: Morgenthau stresses that no Armenian was exempted whatever his class or wealth, which marks targeting by group identity. Nazi Germany's destruction of European Jews during World War II was likewise a state's wartime campaign against a whole people.

options.text: Like the Cambodian genocide, it was led by a communist movement that targeted educated urban residents to build a classless rural agrarian society of peasants.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The Ottoman government was not communist, and the excerpt says victims were targeted regardless of education or social class, not because of them.

facts: Nazi Germany carried out the Holocaust against European Jews during World War II (1939-1945).
The Khmer Rouge genocide in Cambodia (1975-1979) targeted people largely by class and perceived political identity.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The statement that no Armenian was exempted, whatever his education, wealth or class, shows the campaign targeted an entire ethnic group.
design.evidence_quote: Scarcely a single Armenian, whatever his education or wealth, or whatever the social class to which he belonged, was exempted

items.stem: EXTRA. Which of the following best describes Morgenthau's main claim in the excerpt?

options.text: The deportation was aimed mainly at wealthy and educated Armenians in the largest cities, such as Constantinople, Smyrna, and Aleppo.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt says those three cities were spared, and that Armenians of every class were included.

options.text: German military advisers designed the deportation order, while Ottoman officials hid it from foreign diplomats.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt credits the orders to Turkish authorities and says they made little attempt to hide their purpose from Morgenthau.

options.text: The deportation was a sincere resettlement plan that failed because wartime shortages of food and water overwhelmed Ottoman officials.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Morgenthau explicitly denies that the deportation was undertaken in good faith.

options.text: The deportation was a disguised method of killing Armenians rather than a real plan to resettle them in a new region.
options.label: key
options.why: Morgenthau writes that the Turks never meant to reestablish the Armenians and that the real purpose was 'a new method of massacre.'

facts: Ottoman authorities deported Armenians toward the Syrian desert in 1915, and large numbers died on the way or were killed.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Morgenthau rejects the resettlement explanation and names the purpose as massacre.
design.evidence_quote: The real purpose of the deportation was robbery and destruction; it really represented a new method of massacre.

items.stem: EXTRA. Morgenthau's charge that Ottoman orders amounted to a 'death warrant to a whole race' relates most directly to which later development?

options.text: The United Nations convention of 1948 that defined genocide as a crime under international law
options.label: key
options.why: The deliberate destruction of whole peoples, which Morgenthau describes, was later defined in law as genocide. Raphael Lemkin, who cited the Armenian case among his examples, coined the term, and the UN adopted the Genocide Convention in 1948.

options.text: The Geneva Convention of 1864, which set the first international rules for the care of wounded soldiers
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This came decades before 1915, and it addressed wounded soldiers, not attacks on civilian populations.

options.text: The Treaty of Versailles clause of 1919 assigning responsibility for starting the war to Germany and its allies
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The war guilt clause is real, but it concerned the war's outbreak, not the destruction of a people.

options.text: The Treaty of Lausanne of 1923, which created an independent Armenian state covering most of eastern Anatolia
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The Lausanne treaty recognized the Republic of Turkey and created no Armenian state in Anatolia.

facts: Raphael Lemkin coined the term genocide in 1944, citing the fate of the Armenians among his examples.
The United Nations adopted the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide in 1948.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The phrase 'death warrant to a whole race' describes the intentional destruction of a group, the idea later defined in law as genocide.
design.evidence_quote: they were merely giving the death warrant to a whole race

spec.theme: War aims, self-determination and empires at the end of the First World War

sources.context: United States President Woodrow Wilson gave this address to Congress in January 1918, during the First World War.

items.stem: The wording of point V in Wilson's address best reflects which of the following points of view on colonial empires?

options.text: Colonial disputes should be settled by revolutionary uprisings of workers as the Bolsheviks urged
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Calling for revolutionary uprisings against imperialism was the Bolshevik position. Wilson proposed an orderly, impartial settlement between governments instead.

options.text: Colonial rule could be reformed to weigh the interests of colonized peoples
options.label: key
options.why: Point V asks that the interests of colonial populations get equal weight with the claims of governing powers. It does not call for ending colonial rule, which fits Wilson's reformist and gradual approach to empire.

options.text: European empires should be free to expand their colonial holdings as compensation for war losses
options.label: reversal
options.why: This turns the point around. Wilson wanted colonial claims limited by the interests of local populations, not empires growing as war compensation.

options.text: All colonies held by the warring empires should be granted immediate independence after the war
options.label: overstated
options.why: The text calls for an impartial adjustment of colonial claims and still counts the governing power's equitable claims. It never demands immediate independence.

facts: Wilson presented the Fourteen Points to Congress on January 8, 1918.
The Fourteen Points called for adjusting colonial claims, not for the immediate end of colonial empires.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Point V balances the interests of populations against the equitable claims of the governing power, which shows a reformist view rather than an anticolonial one.
design.evidence_quote: the interests of the populations concerned must have equal weight with the equitable claims of the government

items.stem: Wilson's call in point XII for the Dardanelles to be permanently opened is best understood in the context of which wartime development?

options.text: Japan had joined the Allies and seized German-held ports and Pacific islands in the early months of the war
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Japan did take German holdings in East Asia and the Pacific in 1914, but this has nothing to do with the Ottoman straits.

options.text: Turkish nationalists under Mustafa Kemal had abolished the sultanate and moved the capital to Ankara
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: These changes came in 1922 and 1923, years after the January 1918 address.

options.text: The Ottoman Empire had joined the Central Powers and closed the straits to Allied shipping
options.label: key
options.why: The Ottomans entered the war on the side of Germany in 1914 and closed the straits, which cut a sea route to Russia. The Allied Gallipoli campaign of 1915 failed to force them open. That is why opening the Dardanelles was a war aim.

options.text: The Suez Canal had opened in 1869, giving Britain a shorter sea route to its colonies in South Asia
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This is accurate, but the Suez Canal is a different waterway. It does not explain why the Dardanelles needed guarantees in 1918.

facts: The Ottoman Empire entered the First World War on the side of the Central Powers in 1914.
The Allied Gallipoli campaign of 1915 to 1916 failed to force open the Dardanelles.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Point XII singles out the Dardanelles as a passage that needs international guarantees, which reflects the wartime Ottoman closure of the straits.
design.evidence_quote: the Dardanelles should be permanently opened as a free passage to the ships and commerce of all nations

items.stem: Which of the following describes a postwar outcome for many Arab peoples formerly under Ottoman rule that departed from the aims stated in point XII?

options.text: They were taken over by Japan as part of its expanding sphere of influence in the Pacific
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Japan received German Pacific islands as mandates, not former Ottoman Arab lands.

options.text: They were divided between Italy and Greece under the terms of the Treaty of Sevres signed in 1920
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The Treaty of Sevres gave Greece and Italy claims in Anatolia and the Aegean. The Arab lands went to Britain and France as mandates.

options.text: They gained full independence as nation-states guaranteed by the peace treaties signed at Paris
options.label: reversal
options.why: The peace settlement did not give most former Ottoman Arab lands full independence. They were put under European mandate rule.

options.text: They were placed under British and French mandates by the League of Nations
options.label: key
options.why: After the war, lands such as Syria, Lebanon, Iraq and Palestine became League of Nations mandates under France and Britain. This fell short of the autonomous development promised to nationalities under Turkish rule.

facts: After the First World War, the League of Nations mandate system placed Syria and Lebanon under France and Iraq and Palestine under Britain.
