The Treaty of Sevres of 1920 gave Greece and Italy claims in former Ottoman territory in Anatolia and the Aegean.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Point XII promises autonomous development to the nationalities under Turkish rule, and the mandate system departed from that promise.
design.evidence_quote: the other nationalities which are now under Turkish rule should be assured an undoubted security of life

items.stem: Wilson's language about autonomous development and the interests of colonial populations is most directly connected to which of the following developments in 1919?

options.text: Mass protests in Korea and Egypt demanding independence from foreign rule
options.label: key
options.why: Wilsonian ideas of self-determination encouraged the March First Movement in Korea and the 1919 revolution in Egypt. In both, activists demanded an end to foreign rule.

options.text: The Meiji government adopting a constitution modeled on Prussian law to strengthen imperial authority
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Meiji Constitution came in 1889 and had nothing to do with Wilson's wartime ideas.

options.text: The Mexican Revolution producing a constitution that limited foreign ownership of land and oil
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Mexico's 1917 Constitution came out of its own revolution, before the Fourteen Points. It was not a response to Wilson's self-determination language.

options.text: The Indian National Congress launching the Quit India campaign demanding immediate British withdrawal
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Quit India Movement started in 1942, during the Second World War, not in 1919.

facts: The March First Movement for Korean independence from Japan began in 1919.
Egyptian nationalists rose against British control in the 1919 revolution.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The promise of autonomous development for subject nationalities was the kind of language that anticolonial activists cited in 1919.
design.evidence_quote: an absolutely unmolested opportunity of autonomous development

items.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of Wilson's address as evidence for how former Ottoman lands and colonies were actually treated after the war?

options.text: It was delivered after the Treaty of Versailles and so reflects the bargaining of the Paris Peace Conference
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The address dates from January 1918. The Treaty of Versailles was signed in 1919.

options.text: It states aims before the war ended, not the terms the victors later imposed
options.label: key
options.why: The address was given in January 1918, while the war was still being fought. It states aims, not the settlement the victors actually made at Paris in 1919 and 1920.

options.text: It addresses only European boundaries and says nothing about colonies or non-European peoples
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Point V deals with colonial claims, and point XII deals with peoples under Ottoman rule, so the address does discuss non-European peoples.

options.text: It was written by a Central Powers leader seeking to divide the Allied coalition before the end of the war
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The credit line names Wilson, President of the United States, as the author. The United States fought against the Central Powers.

facts: Wilson delivered the Fourteen Points address in January 1918, before the armistice of November 1918.
The Treaty of Versailles was signed in 1919 at the Paris Peace Conference.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line dates the address to January 1918, during the war, and the text speaks of the Ottoman Empire as still existing.
design.evidence_quote: The turkish portion of the present Ottoman Empire should be assured a secure sovereignty

spec.theme: Containment and the beginning of the Cold War

sources.context: United States President Harry Truman gave this address to Congress in March 1947 while asking for aid to Greece and Turkey.

items.stem: The policy Truman proposes in the second part of the excerpt is best understood as an early statement of which of the following Cold War concepts?

options.text: Isolationism, a policy of avoiding entangling commitments in conflicts outside the Western Hemisphere
options.label: reversal
options.why: The address commits the United States to involvement abroad, which breaks with its earlier isolationist tradition.

options.text: Non-alignment, a refusal to join either of the rival blocs led by the superpowers
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Non-alignment was the position of newly independent states such as India and Indonesia. It was not the policy of a superpower committing itself to one side.

options.text: Containment, an effort to limit the expansion of Soviet influence and communism
options.label: key
options.why: Pledging to support free peoples resisting armed minorities or outside pressures, made in the setting of aid to Greece and Turkey, is the classic first statement of containment as United States policy.

options.text: Appeasement, a strategy of granting concessions to expansionist powers to avoid a wider war
options.label: reversal
options.why: Appeasement, linked to Britain and France facing Nazi Germany in the 1930s, means giving way to an expansionist power. Truman proposes resisting outside pressure, which is the opposite.

facts: Truman asked Congress in March 1947 for 400 million dollars in aid to Greece and Turkey, a request that became known as the Truman Doctrine.
The Truman Doctrine is generally treated as the first formal statement of the United States policy of containing Soviet and communist expansion.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Truman's pledge to support peoples resisting subjugation by armed minorities or outside pressures states the goal of containment.
design.evidence_quote: it must be the policy of the United States to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the main argument Truman makes in the excerpt?

options.text: Most nations were by then freely choosing their governments, so outside assistance from the United States was unnecessary
options.label: reversal
options.why: Truman says the choice is too often not a free one, and he uses that point to argue that assistance is needed.

options.text: Colonial powers in Europe should grant immediate independence to their overseas territories in Asia and Africa
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt never mentions colonial empires. Its subject is the contrast between democratic and repressive systems.

options.text: The United States should use its armed forces to overthrow communist governments already established in Eastern Europe
options.label: overstated
options.why: The excerpt calls for supporting peoples who are resisting. It says nothing about overthrowing existing governments or sending American troops into Eastern Europe.

options.text: The world faced a choice between two systems, and the United States should aid peoples resisting coercion
options.label: key
options.why: Truman contrasts two ways of life, one based on majority will and one imposed by a minority, and then argues that the United States should support free peoples resisting subjugation.

facts: The Truman Doctrine of 1947 described a global contest between free and totalitarian systems as the basis for American foreign aid.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt sets out two alternative ways of life and then states a policy of supporting those who resist subjugation.
design.evidence_quote: nearly every nation must choose between alternative ways of life. The choice is too often not a free one.

items.stem: Which of the following developments most directly shaped the situation in which Truman delivered this address?

options.text: A civil war in Greece and Soviet pressure on Turkey as weakened Britain withdrew support
options.label: key
options.why: In early 1947 Britain, drained by the Second World War, said it could no longer support Greece, where the government was fighting communist insurgents. Turkey also faced Soviet demands over the Turkish Straits. These were the reasons Truman asked for aid.

options.text: The partition of British India into the newly independent states of India and Pakistan
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Partition took place in August 1947, but it was a matter of decolonization in South Asia and was not the situation behind a request for aid to Greece and Turkey.

options.text: The Soviet launch of the Sputnik satellite, which intensified fears of a widening missile gap
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Sputnik was launched in 1957, a decade after the address.

options.text: The Korean War, in which United Nations forces fought against North Korean and Chinese troops
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Korean War began in 1950, three years after this 1947 address.

facts: In February 1947 Britain informed the United States that it could no longer afford aid to Greece and Turkey.
The Greek Civil War (1946 to 1949) pitted the Greek government against communist-led insurgents.
After the Second World War the Soviet Union pressed Turkey for control over the Turkish Straits.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line says the address asked for aid to Greece and Turkey, and the text mentions armed minorities and outside pressures.
design.evidence_quote: resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures

items.stem: Truman's contrast between two ways of life most likely served which purpose, given the audience described in the context line?

options.text: To warn Soviet leaders that American atomic weapons would be used against any expansion
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt does not mention atomic weapons or threaten the Soviet Union directly.

options.text: To persuade Congress to fund aid by presenting it as a defense of freedom
options.label: key
options.why: Truman was speaking to Congress to ask for aid. Framing the issue as a choice between liberty and oppression gave lawmakers a moral and ideological reason to approve the money.

options.text: To justify withdrawing the United States from the newly founded United Nations
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the excerpt concerns the United Nations, and the United States stayed a leading member.

options.text: To announce a formal military alliance between North America and Western European states
options.label: misattributed
options.why: That describes NATO, which was founded in 1949. The 1947 address asked for aid to two countries and did not create an alliance.

facts: The Truman Doctrine address was delivered to a joint session of Congress on March 12, 1947, and Congress approved the requested aid in 1947.
NATO was established in 1949.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line identifies Congress as the audience and the purpose as a request for aid, and the text frames that aid in terms of freedom versus oppression.
design.evidence_quote: guarantees of individual liberty, freedom of speech and religion, and freedom from political oppression

items.stem: The policy announced in the excerpt most directly contributed to which of the following later developments in the period 1950 to 1975?

options.text: The rapid independence of most sub-Saharan African colonies from Britain and France around 1960
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: African decolonization came mainly from nationalist movements and the weakness of the European empires after the war, not from the Truman Doctrine.

options.text: The Bandung Conference of 1955, where Asian and African states rejected alignment with either bloc
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Bandung reflected newly independent states keeping their distance from both superpowers. It was not an application of American containment policy.

options.text: American military involvement in Korea and Vietnam to stop the spread of communism
options.label: key
options.why: The commitment to support peoples resisting communist pressure grew into containment policy, which the United States used to justify fighting in Korea from 1950 and in Vietnam during the 1960s and 1970s.

options.text: The 1949 victory of Mao Zedong's Communist forces over the Nationalists in the Chinese Civil War
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Communist victory in China was a setback for containment, not a result of it. It also happened in 1949, before the period named in the stem.

facts: The United States led United Nations forces in the Korean War from 1950 to 1953.
The United States escalated its military involvement in Vietnam in the 1960s, withdrawing combat troops in 1973.
The Bandung Conference of Asian and African states met in 1955.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt's pledge to support peoples resisting outside pressures became the basis of containment, which later justified American interventions in Asia.
design.evidence_quote: I believe that we must assist free peoples to work out their own destinies in their own way.

spec.theme: The path to independence in the Gold Coast

sources.context: This reference book was written for the U.S. government; the country was called the Gold Coast under British rule before it became independent as Ghana in 1957.

spec.theme: China's opening to the world economy in the 1980s

sources.context: This reference book was written for the U.S. government and describes China's economy in the mid-1980s.

items.stem: Which of the following best explains why China's leaders adopted the policy changes described in the excerpt?

options.text: Rules for entry into the World Trade Organization obliged China to open coastal ports to foreign firms and lower its tariffs
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The WTO was founded in 1995, and China joined in 2001. That came long after the special economic zones of 1979 and the opening policy of the early 1980s.

options.text: The collapse of the Soviet Union removed China's main trading partner and forced Beijing to look for new export markets abroad
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, more than a decade after the reforms began in the late 1970s. China had also broken with the Soviets in the Sino-Soviet split around 1960.

options.text: International Monetary Fund lenders required China to privatize state industries as a condition of emergency debt relief
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Structural adjustment conditions were placed on debtor states in Latin America and Africa. China did not adopt its opening policy because of IMF debt conditions, and the excerpt describes the reforms as China's own commitment.

options.text: Post-Mao leaders sought faster growth through market incentives and foreign capital while keeping one-party rule
options.label: key
options.why: After Mao's death in 1976, Deng Xiaoping's leadership reversed the Maoist strategy the excerpt mentions. It used foreign investment, trade and market incentives to modernize the economy, and the Communist Party kept its monopoly on political power.

facts: Deng Xiaoping emerged as China's leader in 1978 and began market-oriented economic reforms.
China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001.
The Soviet Union dissolved in 1991.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt says China 'reversed the Maoist economic development strategy' beginning in the late 1970s, which points to the post-Mao reform leadership.
design.evidence_quote: Beginning in the late 1970s, China reversed the Maoist economic development strategy

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the authors' main claim about China's opening up policy?

options.text: It aided China's economic development and drew the country into the global economy
options.label: key
options.why: The authors state directly that the changes benefited the Chinese economy and also integrated China into the world economy.

options.text: It centralized control over foreign trade in a few Beijing ministries to protect state industry
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt says foreign trade institutions were reorganized and decentralized, not centralized.

options.text: It left China dependent on Western lenders and weakened the Communist Party's control of the economy
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The authors mention involvement in international financial markets, but they make no claim about dependency or weakened party control. Their overall judgment is positive.

options.text: It extended the Maoist goal of national self-reliance by limiting China's need for imported goods
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt says the policy reversed the Maoist strategy. It also stresses the import of foreign technology and the rapid growth of trade.

facts: China's economic reforms that began in 1978 expanded foreign trade and foreign investment during the 1980s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The authors' summary sentence says the changes benefited China's economy and integrated China into the world economy.
design.evidence_quote: These changes not only benefited the Chinese economy but also integrated China into the world economy.

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would most directly support the authors' claim that the opening policy integrated China into the world economy?

options.text: State-owned enterprises still produced most of China's industrial output in the mid-1980s
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This describes domestic ownership. At most it would qualify how far the reforms went; it does not show integration into world markets.

options.text: Foreign direct investment flowing into Shenzhen and other coastal zones grew rapidly during the 1980s
options.label: key
options.why: Fast growth of foreign investment in the special economic zones shows foreign capital linking China to global production and trade. That supports the integration claim.

options.text: Western governments imposed arms embargoes and sanctions on China after the crackdown at Tiananmen Square in 1989
options.label: reversal
options.why: Sanctions after 1989 restricted China's foreign ties for a time, so this evidence would complicate the integration claim rather than support it.

options.text: The household responsibility system let rural families sell surplus crops at market prices after meeting state quotas
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This was a real reform of the period, but it concerns domestic agriculture. It is not evidence of China's ties to the world economy.

facts: Shenzhen was made a special economic zone around 1979-1980 and grew rapidly with foreign investment in the 1980s.
Western governments imposed sanctions on China after the Tiananmen Square crackdown in June 1989.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt lists direct foreign investment and the special economic zones, including Shenzhen, as parts of the policy that integrated China into the world economy.
design.evidence_quote: designed to attract foreign investment, expand exports, and import technology and expertise

items.stem: The policies described in the excerpt are best understood as part of which broader trend of the late twentieth century?

options.text: The Non-Aligned Movement's effort to keep newly independent states out of both Cold War alliance systems
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Non-alignment was a diplomatic stance of the 1950s and 1960s. It does not explain China's economic opening.

options.text: Expanded state planning of heavy industry modeled on the Soviet five-year plans of the 1930s
options.label: reversal
options.why: Soviet-style planning was the model that the Maoist strategy drew on and that China moved away from after the late 1970s.

options.text: A global turn toward market-oriented reforms and freer trade and investment across borders
options.label: key
options.why: In the 1980s and 1990s many states, including Britain under Thatcher, the United States under Reagan and later India in 1991, reduced state controls and opened up to trade and investment. China's opening fits this pattern.

options.text: The spread of import substitution industrialization meant to reduce reliance on manufactured goods from abroad
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Import substitution was mainly a mid-twentieth-century strategy, especially in Latin America. It also cuts against the export-processing goals of China's zones.

facts: Margaret Thatcher (from 1979) and Ronald Reagan (from 1981) promoted free-market policies.
India began major economic liberalization in 1991.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt describes China widening foreign economic relations and trade and taking part in international financial markets, which matches the wider late-twentieth-century move toward market liberalization.
design.evidence_quote: committed itself to a policy of being more open to the outside world and widening foreign economic relations and trade

items.stem: Research for the excerpt was completed in 1987. This fact most limits the excerpt's usefulness to historians studying which of the following?

options.text: The reversal of Maoist economic strategy that began in the late 1970s under new leadership
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The reversal is true history and comes before 1987, so the study's date does not limit its usefulness here.

options.text: How China's foreign trade institutions were reorganized and decentralized after 1979
options.label: reversal
options.why: This happened within the period the study covers, and the excerpt discusses it explicitly.

options.text: The goals that Chinese leaders set for the special economic zones in Guangdong
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt directly describes the zones' purposes, so it is useful for this topic, not limited.

options.text: The effects of China's entry into the World Trade Organization in 2001
options.label: key
options.why: A study finished in 1987 cannot describe events of 2001 or their effects, so it is of little use for that topic.

facts: China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The credit line says the research was completed in 1987, so the study cannot address later events.

items.stem: Which of the following was most similar to the policies described in the excerpt?

options.text: Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986 opened its economy to private enterprise and foreign investment
options.label: key
options.why: Like China, communist Vietnam kept one-party rule but adopted market reforms and welcomed foreign investment beginning in 1986.

options.text: Mexico's government nationalized the holdings of foreign oil companies under President Lazaro Cardenas in 1938
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This 1938 action restricted foreign economic control, the opposite of China's 1980s opening.

options.text: North Korea's leaders promoted the juche ideal of self-reliance and limited trade with capitalist states
options.label: reversal
options.why: Juche self-reliance looks more like the Maoist strategy that China abandoned than like the opening policy.

options.text: Cuba's government nationalized foreign-owned sugar estates and businesses after Castro's revolution of 1959
options.label: reversal
options.why: Nationalizing foreign property is the opposite of attracting foreign investment, and it belongs to an earlier period.

facts: Vietnam launched the Doi Moi economic reforms in 1986.
Mexico nationalized foreign oil companies in 1938 under Lazaro Cardenas.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt describes a communist state opening to foreign investment and trade, a pattern that Vietnam's Doi Moi repeated.
design.evidence_quote: direct foreign investment, the creation of special economic zones

spec.theme: Paper money and state power in Yuan China

sources.context: Marco Polo was a Venetian merchant who spent years in Mongol-ruled China in the 13th century; his account of his travels was written down around 1298 with the help of a writer named Rustichello of Pisa.

items.stem: Which of the following best explains the origins of the paper money system described in the excerpt?

options.text: Chinese officials printed notes to replace the large amounts of American silver that entered China through Manila
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: American silver came through Manila only after the 1570s, long after Polo's time.

options.text: Mongol rulers kept a system of state paper currency that had first developed under the Song dynasty
options.label: key
options.why: The Song state issued paper notes beginning in the 11th century, and the Yuan under Khubilai took over and extended this Chinese practice, as the excerpt's description of the Kaan's mint shows.

options.text: Venetian merchants introduced bills of exchange to Yuan officials, who turned them into an official currency
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Polo, a Venetian, is amazed by the notes. That shows they were not a European import, and Chinese paper money came before Yuan contact with Venice.

options.text: Mongol rulers brought a steppe tradition of credit tokens from Central Asia and imposed it on Chinese merchants
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Paper money did not come from steppe traditions. It came out of Chinese commercial and state practice under the Song.

facts: The Song dynasty issued government paper money beginning in the early 11th century.
Khubilai Khan's Yuan government issued paper currency starting in 1260.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The description of a state mint at the Yuan capital making notes from mulberry bark is tied to Chinese paper money, which began under the Song.
design.evidence_quote: The Emperor’s Mint then is in this same City of Cambaluc

items.stem: Polo's comparison of the Kaan's mint to having "the Secret of Alchemy" most likely reflects which of the following?

options.text: His Christian belief that the Great Kaan practiced forms of magic that the Church in Rome had condemned
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The alchemy comparison expresses wonder at a money system that costs nothing to make. It does not accuse the Kaan of forbidden magic.

options.text: His plan to persuade the Venetian government to issue paper notes to pay for its long wars against Genoa
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the excerpt or the context line shows a policy purpose aimed at Venice.

options.text: His background as a European merchant used to coins of gold and silver, not state-issued paper notes
options.label: key
options.why: Medieval Venice used metal coinage. A merchant from there would see paper turned into accepted money as something like turning base matter into gold, which is the point of the alchemy comparison.

options.text: His training in the Confucian examination system, which taught scholar-officials to distrust money made of paper
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Polo was a Venetian merchant, not a Chinese scholar-official trained for the examinations.

facts: Late medieval Venice used gold and silver coinage, including the gold ducat first minted in 1284.
Marco Polo was in Yuan China from about 1275 to about 1292.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The alchemy comparison, together with the context line identifying Polo as a Venetian merchant, shows his outsider's amazement at paper used as money.
design.evidence_quote: you might say he hath the Secret of Alchemy in perfection, and you would be right!

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a claim Polo makes about the Great Kaan's paper money?

options.text: It circulated mainly among foreign merchants on the Silk Roads rather than among the Kaan's own subjects
options.label: reversal
options.why: Polo says the notes passed current universally over all the Kaan's kingdoms and provinces.

options.text: It was costly for the treasury to make because suitable mulberry bark was scarce in northern China
options.label: reversal
options.why: Polo says the money costs the Kaan nothing and that whole districts are full of mulberry trees.

options.text: Its value came from reserves of gold and silver bullion that the emperor kept stored at the mint in Cambaluc
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt never mentions bullion reserves. It links acceptance to the ruler's power.

options.text: Its acceptance across the empire rested on the ruler's authority and the threat of punishment
options.label: key
options.why: Polo says the notes passed current wherever the Kaan's sovereignty extended and that no one dared refuse them on pain of death.

facts: The Yuan government made its paper currency official legal tender throughout its territories in China.
Khubilai Khan ruled the Yuan dynasty from his capital at Khanbaliq (Cambaluc, modern Beijing).

design.key_evidence_in_source: The closing lines tie circulation to the Kaan's sovereignty and the death penalty for refusing the notes.
design.evidence_quote: nobody, however important he may think himself, dares to refuse them on pain of death

items.stem: Which of the following developments in fourteenth-century China was most directly connected to the monetary practice Polo describes?

options.text: Overprinting of notes fed inflation that weakened Yuan rule before the dynasty fell in 1368
options.label: key
options.why: Polo notes that the Kaan printed vast amounts of money that cost him nothing. Later Yuan governments overissued notes, which caused inflation and added to the unrest that ended in the Ming takeover in 1368.

options.text: Yuan rulers abolished paper notes and required merchants to pay all of their commercial taxes in raw silk
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Yuan kept issuing paper money until the dynasty ended. Overissue, not abolition, was the problem.

options.text: Italian city-states such as Venice replaced their gold and silver coins with Mongol-style paper notes
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Italian states kept using metal coinage. Polo's wonder shows that paper money was foreign to Europeans.

options.text: Stable paper money let the Yuan avoid peasant revolts and keep control of China into the sixteenth century
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Yuan faced major revolts, including the Red Turban uprisings, and was overthrown by the Ming in 1368.

facts: Overissue of paper currency in the later Yuan period caused serious inflation in the 14th century.
The Yuan dynasty was overthrown and the Ming dynasty founded in 1368.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Polo's remark that the Kaan made a vast quantity of money every year at no cost points to the later problem of overissue and inflation.
design.evidence_quote: the Kaan causes every year to be made such a vast quantity of this money, which costs him nothing

items.stem: EXTRA. Which of the following broader developments most directly made possible Polo's journey to the Mongol capital described in the excerpt?

options.text: Portuguese voyages around the southern tip of Africa that opened a direct sea route from Europe to East Asia
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Portuguese ships reached India only in 1498, two centuries after Polo.

options.text: Mongol conquests that linked much of Eurasia and protected merchants on overland trade routes
options.label: key
options.why: The Mongol empires unified much of Eurasia in the 13th century and made overland travel safer, which allowed Venetian merchants like the Polos to reach the Yuan court.

options.text: Crusader states in the Levant that gave Venetian traders direct overland access to the Chinese interior
options.label: overstated
options.why: The Crusader states were small coastal territories. They did not open routes to China, and the last of them fell in 1291.

options.text: Ming dynasty treasure fleets under Zheng He that carried foreign envoys and traders to Chinese ports
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Zheng He's voyages took place from 1405 to 1433, more than a century after Polo's travels.

facts: Mongol conquests in the 13th century created a vast Eurasian empire that encouraged overland trade along the Silk Roads.
Zheng He's naval expeditions took place between 1405 and 1433.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line places a Venetian merchant in Mongol-ruled China in the 13th century, which reflects Mongol-era trans-Eurasian connections.

items.stem: EXTRA. Which of the following most limits the use of the excerpt as evidence of how the Yuan monetary system actually worked?

options.text: It describes only how the notes were made and says nothing about how they were used in daily payments
options.label: reversal
options.why: Polo explains that the notes were used for all payments and passed current throughout the empire.

options.text: It was composed centuries after the Yuan dynasty fell, using only secondhand reports from Muslim traders
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The account dates to around 1298, during Yuan rule, and is based on Polo's own stay in China.

options.text: It was dictated after Polo left China and exaggerates how much money the Kaan produced
options.label: key
options.why: According to the context line, the account was written down around 1298, after Polo's return. The claim that the notes equal all the treasure in the world is plainly exaggerated, so its details must be used with caution.

options.text: It was written by a Chinese official who wanted to hide the government's monetary problems from the emperor
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The author was a Venetian merchant, not a Chinese official.

facts: Marco Polo returned to Venice in 1295, and his account was written down with Rustichello of Pisa around 1298.
The Yuan dynasty ruled China until 1368.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line's date and method of composition, together with the hyperbolic claim about the amount of money, limit the excerpt's reliability.
design.evidence_quote: it must equal in amount all the treasure in the world

spec.theme: World population change across the period of the Mongol empire and the Black Death

sources.context: The U.S. Census Bureau publishes a table comparing estimates of world population made by several scholars; this table shows the lowest and highest of those estimates for six years.

items.stem: The difference between the upper estimates for 1200 and 1300 in the table is most consistent with which of the following developments of the thirteenth century?

options.text: Ottoman conquest of Constantinople that ended Byzantine rule over the city
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Constantinople fell in 1453, long after 1300, and that one siege could not account for a change in world population.

options.text: Arrival of smallpox among Indigenous peoples during Spanish colonization of the Caribbean
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Smallpox epidemics in the Americas began after 1492, two centuries after the interval in the question.

options.text: Spread of maize and potatoes from the Americas into Afro-Eurasian farming
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: American crops reached Afro-Eurasia only through the Columbian Exchange after 1492. They also raised population; they did not lower it.

options.text: Mongol conquests that destroyed cities and farmland across Eurasia
options.label: key
options.why: The upper estimate drops from 450 to 432 million between 1200 and 1300. In that century, Mongol campaigns in Central Asia, Persia, northern China and Russia killed large numbers of people and wrecked irrigation and cities, for example at Baghdad in 1258.

facts: Mongol armies conquered much of Eurasia in the 1200s, and the conquests caused mass deaths in Central Asia, Persia and northern China.
The Mongols sacked Baghdad in 1258.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The upper estimate falls from 450 million (1200 AD) to 432 million (1300 AD), and that century matches the Mongol conquests.
design.evidence_quote: Estimated world population, 1000-1500

items.stem: Which of the following best explains how the Mongol Empire contributed to the change in the estimates between 1300 and 1400?

options.text: Its linked trade routes let disease travel quickly across Eurasia
options.label: key
options.why: Mongol control kept overland routes across Eurasia connected and relatively secure. Merchants, soldiers and their goods carried plague from Central Asia to the Black Sea, the Mediterranean and beyond in the 1340s. This explains why both estimates fall by 1400.

options.text: Its tribute demands drove millions to migrate by sea to the Americas
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: No migration from Eurasia to the Americas took place in the 1300s. European colonization began after 1492.

options.text: Its khans banned foreign merchants, cutting off grain imports to cities in China
options.label: reversal
options.why: Mongol rulers generally protected and encouraged long-distance merchants. They did not ban them.

options.text: Its rulers forced peasants onto plantations growing export crops
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Plantation export farming does not describe Mongol rule. It belongs to later Atlantic colonial economies.

facts: The Pax Mongolica of the 1200s and 1300s made trade and travel easier across Eurasia.
The Black Death spread from Central Asia to the Black Sea region and then to the Mediterranean, Europe and North Africa in the 1340s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Both estimates fall between 1300 AD (360 to 432) and 1400 AD (350 to 374). That is the century of plague spread along Mongol-era routes.
design.evidence_quote: Estimated world population, 1000-1500

items.stem: Which of the following data from the table best supports a historian's claim that world population fell during the fourteenth century?

options.text: The upper estimate falls from 345 million in 1000 AD to 320 million in 1100 AD
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This decline is in the eleventh century, not the fourteenth. The lower estimate actually rises in that interval.

options.text: Both estimates drop between 1300 and 1400, the upper by 58 million
options.label: key
options.why: The fourteenth century runs from 1300 to 1400. The lower estimate goes from 360 to 350 million and the upper from 432 to 374 million. So scholars at both ends of the range record a decline.

options.text: Both estimates rise between 1400 and 1500, the upper by 166 million
options.label: reversal
options.why: This shows growth in the fifteenth century, which is the opposite of the claimed decline and in a different period.

options.text: The lower estimate holds at 360 million from 1200 through the year 1300
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This figure is accurate, but it covers the thirteenth century and shows no change, not a fall.

facts: The fourteenth century covers the years 1301 to 1400 and includes the Black Death of the 1340s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Computation: upper estimate 432 (1300 AD) minus 374 (1400 AD) equals 58 million. The lower estimate also falls, from 360 to 350.
design.evidence_quote: Estimated world population, 1000-1500

items.stem: The rise in both estimates between 1000 and 1200 is best understood in the context of which broader development of that period?

options.text: The Atlantic slave trade shifting millions of African laborers to plantations in Brazil
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Atlantic slave trade to Brazil began in the 1500s. Moving forced laborers would also not raise world population.

options.text: Mechanized textile factories drawing rural workers into fast-growing cities
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Mechanized factories came with industrialization in the late 1700s and 1800s.

options.text: Expanding farm output, aided by fast-ripening Champa rice in Song China
options.label: key
options.why: Both estimates rise between 1000 and 1200 (lower from 254 to 360 million). In Song China, which held a large share of world population, fast-ripening, drought-resistant Champa rice made double cropping possible and increased the food supply.

options.text: The Columbian Exchange carrying American food crops into Africa and Asia
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Columbian Exchange began after 1492, so it cannot explain growth before 1200.

facts: Champa rice, a fast-ripening rice from Southeast Asia, was promoted in Song China in the early 1000s.
Song China's population grew significantly in the 11th and 12th centuries.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The lower estimate rises from 254 (1000 AD) to 360 (1200 AD), and the upper from 345 to 450.
design.evidence_quote: Estimated world population, 1000-1500

items.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of the table for a historian studying the demographic effects of the Black Death?

options.text: It counts only the population of Europe, leaving out Asia and Africa
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The table's title says it gives world population estimates.

options.text: It relies on one scholar's figures alone, so it shows no disagreement among experts
options.label: reversal
options.why: The table shows the lowest and highest of several scholars' estimates, so it does display disagreement.

options.text: It reports only figures gathered by the census takers of the Mongol court
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The credit line says the figures are modern scholars' estimates collected by the U.S. Census Bureau, not Mongol records.

options.text: Its century intervals hide sharp short-term drops like those of the 1340s
options.label: key
options.why: The table gives figures only for every hundredth year. A historian therefore cannot see the drop during and right after the plague of the 1340s, which was partly offset by the end of the century.

facts: The Black Death struck Eurasia and North Africa mainly between 1346 and 1353.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line says the table shows estimates for six years, spaced a century apart, so the 1340s cannot be seen.
design.evidence_quote: this table shows the lowest and highest of those estimates for six years

items.stem: In western Europe, the population decline reflected in the estimates between 1300 and 1400 most directly led to which of the following?

options.text: Labor shortages that raised wages and weakened serfdom
options.label: key
options.why: The plague killed a large part of Europe's population. Surviving peasants and workers could demand higher wages and better terms, which weakened serfdom in western Europe.

options.text: Rapid growth of factory towns powered by coal and steam engines
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Coal- and steam-powered factory towns came with the Industrial Revolution of the 1700s and 1800s.

options.text: Expansion of plantation slavery in the Caribbean sugar colonies
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Caribbean sugar plantations grew after European colonization in the 1500s and 1600s.

options.text: The launching of the First Crusade to recover Jerusalem
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The First Crusade began in 1095, centuries before the fourteenth-century decline.

facts: The Black Death killed roughly a third or more of Europe's population in the mid-1300s.
Labor shortages after the plague raised wages and contributed to the decline of serfdom in western Europe.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The upper estimate falls from 432 (1300 AD) to 374 (1400 AD), which reflects the plague-era population loss.
design.evidence_quote: Estimated world population, 1000-1500

spec.theme: Mughal court painting, religion and the foreign rulers it shows

sources.context: This painting was made around 1615 to 1618 for Jahangir, the Mughal emperor of India, by the court painter Bichitr.

items.stem: Based on its title and imagery, which of the following best describes the purpose of the painting made for Jahangir by his court painter Bichitr?

options.text: To criticize the emperor for neglecting affairs of state while spending his time with religious mystics
options.label: reversal
options.why: The emperor's own court painter made the work for him, and it praises the emperor's choice rather than criticizing it.

options.text: To glorify the emperor as a ruler whose spiritual devotion placed him above other monarchs
options.label: key
options.why: The title says Jahangir prefers a Sufi shaikh to kings. The halo and the raised hourglass throne put him above the kings shown below, so the court painting praises his piety and his rank.

options.text: To encourage Mughal subjects to convert to Christianity by including angels drawn from European religious art
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The winged figures borrow European artistic motifs. The central act, though, is the emperor honoring a Muslim Sufi shaikh, and nothing in the painting promotes conversion.

options.text: To record the terms of a commercial treaty that the Mughal emperor signed with the English crown
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: A European figure appears, but nothing in the image or caption points to a treaty. It is a symbolic court image, not a diplomatic record.

facts: Jahangir ruled the Mughal Empire from 1605 to 1627.
Mughal emperors commissioned court paintings to present an idealized image of imperial authority.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The title says the emperor prefers a Sufi shaikh to kings, and the halo and raised throne set him above everyone else in the image.
design.evidence_quote: Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings

items.stem: Showing kings, including a man in European dress, placed below the haloed emperor most directly suggests which claim about Jahangir?

options.text: Sufi orders controlled tax collection in Mughal provinces
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The shaikh receives a book as a mark of honor. Nothing in the image concerns revenue, and Mughal taxes were handled by imperial officials such as zamindars and mansabdars.

options.text: European monarchs and the Mughal emperor governed as equal partners in a shared Indian Ocean trade system
options.label: overstated
options.why: The composition shows a ranking, not equality, and the image says nothing about shared government of trade.

options.text: The Mughal emperor held higher status than the Ottoman and European rulers of his day
options.label: key
options.why: The kings stand lower in the picture than the emperor. He sits on a raised throne in front of a large halo, and the title says he prefers the shaikh to them. Together these features claim that Mughal rank is higher than theirs.

options.text: The Mughal emperor accepted the Ottoman sultan's authority as caliph over all Sunni Muslim rulers
options.label: reversal
options.why: The painting puts the other rulers below Jahangir, which makes the opposite claim. The Mughals did not submit to Ottoman authority.

facts: Mughal revenue collection relied on imperial officials and zamindars, not Sufi orders.
Jahangir ruled from 1605 to 1627, a period when Ottoman sultans and the English king James I were also on the throne.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The kings are placed lower in the picture than the haloed emperor on his raised hourglass throne, and the title says he prefers the shaikh to kings.
design.evidence_quote: Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings

items.stem: The European-dressed monarch and the European-style winged figures in this c. 1615-1618 painting most directly reflect which historical context?

options.text: Spanish missionaries had converted the Mughal ruling family to Catholicism after the conquest of the Philippines
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Jesuits did visit the Mughal court, but the Mughal dynasty stayed Muslim, and the Spanish Philippines had nothing to do with Mughal religion.

options.text: Mughal rulers had banned all European traders from Indian ports to protect local merchants
options.label: reversal
options.why: Jahangir allowed European trade. The English, for example, set up a trading post at Surat during his reign.

options.text: The British East India Company had taken control of Bengal's revenue after its military victory at Plassey
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Battle of Plassey was fought in 1757, more than a century after this painting was made.

options.text: English and other European envoys and merchants were seeking trade privileges at the Mughal court
options.label: key
options.why: In the early 1600s the English East India Company, the Portuguese and others sought trading rights from the Mughals. James I's ambassador Sir Thomas Roe was at Jahangir's court from 1615 to 1619, and European prints and art also reached the court.

facts: Sir Thomas Roe served as James I's ambassador to Jahangir's court from 1615 to 1619.
The English East India Company was chartered in 1600 and set up a trading post at Surat in the 1610s.
The Battle of Plassey took place in 1757.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The painting's date (c. 1615-1618) and the European-dressed monarch and cherubs connect it to European diplomatic and trade contacts with Jahangir's court.

items.stem: The painting's image of an emperor honoring a Sufi holy man most directly continued which earlier approach to ruling the religiously diverse Mughal Empire?

options.text: Akbar's veneration of Chishti Sufi saints and his sponsorship of debates among many faiths
options.label: key
options.why: Akbar, Jahangir's father, honored Chishti saints and held religious debates at his court. He also abolished the jizya in 1564. Jahangir's public respect for a Sufi shaikh continues that approach.

options.text: The Ottoman devshirme system of taking Christian boys from the Balkans to serve
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The devshirme was an Ottoman way of recruiting soldiers and officials. It has no connection to Mughal patronage of Sufi saints.

options.text: The Safavid shahs' policy of making Twelver Shia Islam the official faith of their Persian empire
options.label: misattributed
options.why: This was a Safavid policy of enforcing one faith, not a Mughal approach to governing a diverse population.

options.text: Aurangzeb's later reimposition of the jizya on non-Muslims and his support for stricter enforcement of Islamic law
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Aurangzeb ruled after Jahangir and brought back the jizya in 1679, so his policy could not be an earlier approach that Jahangir continued. It also broke from the policies of Akbar and Jahangir.

facts: Akbar abolished the jizya in 1564 and hosted interfaith debates beginning in the 1570s.
Akbar honored the Chishti Sufi order, including Salim Chishti at Fatehpur Sikri.
Aurangzeb reimposed the jizya in 1679.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The emperor handing a book to the white-bearded Sufi shaikh, along with the title, shows imperial honor given to a Sufi holy man.
design.evidence_quote: Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings

items.stem: EXTRA. The white-bearded man receiving the book represents a Sufi shaikh. In South Asia during this era, Sufi orders contributed most directly to which development?

options.text: The enforcement of uniform Islamic law by state-appointed judges in every Mughal province
options.label: reversal
options.why: Sufism stressed mystical devotion over strict legal uniformity, and judges were state officials, not Sufi shaikhs.

options.text: The spread of Islam through devotional practices that adapted to local cultures
options.label: key
options.why: Sufi mystics, with their shrines, devotional music and emphasis on personal devotion, attracted followers and helped spread Islam across South Asia. Mughal rulers often honored Sufis, as this painting shows.

options.text: The military conquest of northern India by Babur's armies at the Battle of Panipat
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Babur won at Panipat in 1526 with gunpowder armies, not through Sufi orders.

options.text: The rise of the Bhakti movement, which rejected caste and called for devotion to Hindu deities
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Bhakti was a Hindu devotional movement. It ran alongside Sufism and shared some features with it, but Sufi orders did not create it.

facts: Sufi orders such as the Chishtiyya helped spread Islam in South Asia through shrines and devotional practice.
Babur defeated the Delhi Sultanate at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The title identifies the old man as a Sufi shaikh, and the emperor honors him by handing him a book.
design.evidence_quote: Sufi Shaikh

items.stem: EXTRA. Which of the following most limits the painting's usefulness as evidence of how Mughal India actually related to foreign powers?

options.text: Its Persian inscriptions were added by later British collectors who misread the scene and its figures
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the credit or context line says the inscriptions were added later. The calligraphy is part of the Mughal album page.

options.text: It was produced by a European artist who had never traveled to or seen the Indian subcontinent
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The credit line names Bichitr, a Mughal court painter, as the artist.

options.text: It was made for Jahangir's court and presents the emperor's ideal image of his own status
options.label: key
options.why: The context line says the painting was made for Jahangir by his court painter. It shows the emperor's preferred picture of his rank, not how foreign rulers actually saw him or dealt with him.

options.text: It was painted after the Mughals had lost most of their territory to the Maratha Confederacy
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The painting dates to c. 1615-1618. The Maratha gains came in the 1700s.

facts: Bichitr was a painter at Jahangir's court in the early 1600s.
The Maratha Confederacy expanded at Mughal expense mainly in the 1700s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line says the painting was made for Jahangir by his own court painter, which points to an idealized view from the court.

spec.theme: Law, religion and foreigners in the Ottoman Empire

sources.context: Albert Lybyer was an American historian who wrote this study of the Ottoman government in the time of Sultan Suleiman, who ruled from 1520 to 1566.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes Lybyer's main claim about how the Ottomans governed their non-Muslim subjects?

options.text: Ottoman rulers gave non-Muslim subjects the same legal status and tax obligations as Muslim subjects.
options.label: overstated
options.why: The excerpt draws a clear line between Muslim citizens and non-Muslim subjects. It describes separate status, not equality.

options.text: Ottoman rulers separated religion from law, following the model of states in western Europe.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Lybyer says the system is hard to grasp in a land that has separated religion and law. In the Ottoman case the two were united.

options.text: Ottoman rulers applied a single Islamic legal code equally to every subject regardless of faith.
options.label: reversal
options.why: This is the opposite of the excerpt, which says people of different faiths lived under different laws.

options.text: Ottoman rulers let large non-Muslim communities use their own law in internal matters.
options.label: key
options.why: Lybyer says the Ottomans left Greek Orthodox, Armenian, Jewish and other communities their own religion, their own law and its administration in matters not involving Muslims.

facts: Ottoman non-Muslim communities such as the Greek Orthodox, Armenians and Jews were allowed communal religious and legal autonomy in internal matters, a pattern later called the millet system.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt states that the Ottomans left each large non-Muslim body to its own religion, law and legal administration.
design.evidence_quote: not merely to its own religion, but to its own law and the administration of its law in all matters that did not concern Moslems

items.stem: Which of the following historical developments would best support Lybyer's argument about the Ottoman treatment of non-Muslim communities?

options.text: Mehmed II recognized a Greek Orthodox patriarch to lead his community after taking Constantinople.
options.label: key
options.why: When Mehmed II named a patriarch to head the Orthodox community after 1453, he gave that community its own religious and legal leadership. This is the arrangement Lybyer describes.

options.text: Ottoman armies used gunpowder cannon to breach Constantinople's walls in 1453 and to besiege Vienna in 1529.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: These were military expansion events. They say nothing about legal autonomy for religious communities.

options.text: Suleiman issued kanun law codes that regulated taxation, land grants, and criminal penalties across the provinces.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Suleiman's kanun codes were sultanic state law. They do not show non-Muslim communities running their own legal affairs.

options.text: The devshirme system took Christian boys from Balkan villages, converted them, and trained them for state service.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The devshirme was real, but it took boys out of their communities and converted them. It does not show communities being left to their own law, and it would complicate Lybyer's picture more than support it.

facts: Mehmed II conquered Constantinople in 1453 and in 1454 installed Gennadios Scholarios as Greek Orthodox patriarch.
The devshirme levied Christian boys for conversion and state service from the late 1300s into the 1600s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Lybyer's argument that the Greek Orthodox and others were left to their own religion and law is supported by the Ottoman recognition of an Orthodox patriarch as community head.
design.evidence_quote: Greek Orthodox, United Greek, Armenian, and Jewish, they left, in time, not merely to its own religion

items.stem: The privileges for foreign residents described at the end of the excerpt are best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.text: Ottoman campaigns into Hungary after the victory at Mohacs in 1526, which brought Christian lands under direct rule
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Mohacs and the expansion into Hungary are real events of Suleiman's reign, but they concern conquered subjects, not privileged foreign residents.

options.text: Ottoman grants of trade privileges, known as capitulations, to European states such as France
options.label: key
options.why: The capitulations gave European merchants living in the empire exemptions and the right to use their own consuls and laws. This matches the foreigners Lybyer describes as almost free from Ottoman control.

options.text: Ottoman policies that closed the empire's ports to Europeans, similar to restrictions adopted by Tokugawa Japan
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Ottomans welcomed European merchants and gave them privileges. Strict restriction of foreign contact was a Tokugawa policy, not an Ottoman one.

options.text: Nineteenth-century Tanzimat reforms that declared Muslim and non-Muslim subjects equal before Ottoman law
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Tanzimat came in the 1800s, long after Suleiman, and it dealt with Ottoman subjects rather than foreign residents.

facts: Suleiman negotiated a commercial and diplomatic agreement with France in 1536, and formal capitulations were granted to France in 1569.
The Tanzimat reforms began in 1839.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt describes foreigners who paid only land tax and customs and were largely free of Ottoman control, which is what the capitulations provided.
design.evidence_quote: they granted even greater privileges to foreigners who wished to reside within the empire

items.stem: The Ottoman policy toward non-Muslim communities described in the excerpt was most similar to which policy in another land-based empire of the period 1450 to 1750?

options.text: Tokugawa shoguns' ban on Christianity and expulsion of Catholic missionaries from Japan in the early 1600s
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Tokugawa suppressed a minority faith. This contrasts with Ottoman toleration and does not resemble it.

options.text: Shah Ismail's campaign to make Twelver Shia Islam the required faith of subjects in the Safavid Empire
options.label: reversal
options.why: Ismail imposed one form of Islam on his subjects instead of tolerating separate religious communities.

options.text: Akbar's abolition of the jizya and tolerance of Hindu subjects in the Mughal Empire
options.label: key
options.why: Akbar, like the Ottomans, was a Muslim ruler who accommodated a large non-Muslim population instead of imposing religious uniformity on it.

options.text: Ferdinand and Isabella's 1492 order expelling Jews who refused to convert from the Spanish kingdoms
options.label: reversal
options.why: Spain enforced religious uniformity by expelling Jews. That is the opposite of the Ottoman acceptance of Jewish communities.

facts: Akbar abolished the jizya on non-Muslims in 1564.
Spain expelled Jews who would not convert in 1492.
Shah Ismail I founded the Safavid state in 1501 and made Twelver Shiism the official religion.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt's description of non-Muslim communities keeping their own religion and law points to a pattern of Muslim rulers accommodating religious diversity.
design.evidence_quote: they left, in time, not merely to its own religion, but to its own law

items.stem: Based on the credit line and context, which of the following is a possible limitation of Lybyer's study as evidence about non-Muslim life in the Ottoman Empire?

options.text: Because Lybyer served as an official at Suleiman's court, he may have exaggerated the generosity of Ottoman law
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Lybyer was an American historian writing in 1913, centuries after Suleiman's reign, which ended in 1566.

options.text: As an American scholar, he could not have consulted any Ottoman documents and relied only on European travel accounts
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the credit line or context says what sources he used, so this claim has no basis.

options.text: Because Lybyer wrote after the Ottoman Empire collapsed in 1922, he may have judged its laws by its final defeat
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The book was published in 1913, before the empire ended in 1922.

options.text: As a study of government, it may show the legal system as designed more than as non-Muslims lived it
options.label: key
options.why: The title shows the book is about the government. It describes the system from the point of view of the state, so it may not show how ordinary non-Muslims experienced it in practice.

facts: Suleiman ruled from 1520 to 1566.
The Ottoman sultanate was abolished in 1922.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The credit line gives a 1913 study titled The Government of the Ottoman Empire by an American historian, which suggests a focus on state structures.

items.stem: In the excerpt, the term Zimmi refers to protected non-Muslim subjects. Which practice most directly defined that status in Islamic states such as the Ottoman Empire?

options.text: Payment of a special head tax in return for protection and freedom of worship
options.label: key
options.why: Dhimmi (Zimmi) status meant non-Muslims paid the jizya and in return received protection and the right to practice their faith.

options.text: Membership in hereditary occupational castes that fixed each family's rank and permitted marriages
options.label: misattributed
options.why: This describes the caste system of South Asia, not the Islamic legal category of protected non-Muslims.

options.text: A complete ban on non-Muslims taking part in long-distance trade or holding any wealth in cities
options.label: overstated
options.why: Non-Muslims faced some restrictions, but many Greek, Armenian and Jewish subjects were prominent merchants.

options.text: Required conversion to Islam within a generation as the condition for keeping land and property
options.label: reversal
options.why: Dhimmi status existed so that non-Muslims could keep their religion. It did not require them to convert.

facts: Under Islamic law, dhimmis (protected non-Muslims, mainly Christians and Jews) paid the jizya head tax in exchange for protection and freedom of worship.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt draws a line between Muslim citizens and non-Muslim subjects (Zimmi), a status defined by the jizya and protection.
design.evidence_quote: drawing a single line between Moslem citizens (Muslim) and non-Moslem subjects (Zimmi)

spec.theme: The Atlantic slave trade and the British campaign against it

sources.context: Opponents of the slave trade printed this plan in 1788 to show how people were packed on the British ship Brookes after a new British law limited the number allowed on board.

items.stem: Which of the following best explains the purpose of the plan of the ship Brookes?

options.text: To convince Parliament to abolish slavery itself throughout Britain's Caribbean colonies at once
options.label: overstated
options.why: The society's name shows it targeted the slave trade. Ending slavery itself in British colonies was a later goal, achieved only in 1833.

options.text: To persuade the British public that the slave trade was cruel even under the new legal limits
options.label: key
options.why: An abolition society printed the plan right after the 1788 law, and it shows captives packed tightly even at the legally permitted number. The goal was to turn public opinion against the trade.

options.text: To advertise the large carrying capacity of British ships to merchants investing in Atlantic voyages
options.label: reversal
options.why: This reverses the plan's meaning. Its creators opposed the trade and used the crowding to condemn it, not to promote investment.

options.text: To guide ship captains in loading captives efficiently so as to comply with the new parliamentary limits
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The credit line names an abolition society as the publisher, not traders or ship officers. The plan was meant to shock readers, not to instruct crews.

facts: The Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade was founded in London in 1787.
Parliament passed the Slave Trade Act (Dolben's Act) in 1788, limiting the number of captives a ship could carry relative to its tonnage.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The credit line names the Plymouth abolition society, and the context line says opponents printed the plan after a law limited numbers on board.
design.evidence_quote: Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade

items.stem: Which of the following claims is most directly made by the printed headings on the plan of the Brookes?

options.text: Captives were kept mostly on the open upper deck, where store rooms and guns blocked any escape
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Both headings describe the lower deck. Nothing in the plan says captives were held mainly on an open upper deck.

options.text: Captives were given more space after 1788 because Parliament had made the crossing safe and humane
options.label: reversal
options.why: The plan was printed to show that conditions stayed brutal under the 1788 limits, which is the opposite of this claim.

options.text: Captives were crowded into spaces with little more than two and a half feet of headroom
options.label: key
options.why: The heading says captives on and below the shelves had only 2 feet 7 inches between the beams, and far less under them.

options.text: Captives were separated by sex and age so that families from the same region could remain together
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The plan does mark separate areas for women, boys and men, but nothing in it says families or people from one region were kept together. Splitting people by sex actually separated families.

facts: Captives on the Middle Passage were usually held below deck in very cramped conditions for voyages lasting weeks or months.
Abolitionists used the Brookes plan in their campaign beginning in 1788 and 1789.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The second heading gives the measurement of 2 feet 7 inches of height for captives stowed on and under the shelves.
design.evidence_quote: HAVE ONLY A HEIGHT OF 2 FEET 7 INCHES BETWEEN THE BEAMS: AND FAR LESS UNDER THE BEAMS

items.stem: The crowding of captives shown in the plan is best understood in the context of which broader development of the period?

options.text: The spread of indentured servitude from South Asia to plantations across the British Empire
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Large-scale South Asian indentured labor began after Britain abolished slavery in the 1830s, decades after this plan.

options.text: Growing Ottoman reliance on the devshirme to supply soldiers and officials from Balkan Christian families
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The devshirme was a real system of forced recruitment in the Ottoman Empire, but it had nothing to do with Atlantic plantation labor.

options.text: Spanish use of the encomienda and mita systems to draw labor from Indigenous communities in the Andes
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: These were real colonial labor systems, but they forced Indigenous Americans to work. They did not drive the shipping of Africans across the Atlantic.

options.text: Rising demand for enslaved labor on sugar plantations in the Caribbean and Brazil
options.label: key
options.why: Sugar plantations in the Caribbean and Brazil had very high death rates and kept demanding new workers. That demand drove traders to pack as many captives as possible onto ships like the Brookes.

facts: Most enslaved Africans carried across the Atlantic were taken to Brazil and the Caribbean, mainly to work on sugar plantations.
High death rates on sugar plantations created continuing demand for new enslaved workers in the 1600s and 1700s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The plan shows hundreds of captives packed onto one ship's lower deck, which reflects the large-scale demand for enslaved labor in the Americas.
design.evidence_quote: PLAN OF LOWER DECK WITH THE STOWAGE OF 292 SLAVES

items.stem: Campaigns like the one that produced this 1788 plan most directly contributed to which later development?

options.text: Britain's 1807 law banning British subjects from taking part in the slave trade
options.label: key
options.why: British abolitionist campaigns, which used images like the Brookes plan, helped bring about the Abolition of the Slave Trade Act of 1807.

options.text: The Haitian Revolution, which British abolitionists organized and led from bases in Jamaica
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Enslaved and free people of color in French Saint-Domingue led the Haitian Revolution beginning in 1791. British abolitionists did not organize it.

options.text: The abolition of slavery in Britain's Caribbean colonies in the same year the Brookes plan appeared
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Britain abolished slavery in its colonies through the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833, not in 1788.

options.text: The immediate end of the transatlantic slave trade to all American ports by the early 1810s
options.label: overstated
options.why: The trade to Brazil and Cuba continued for decades after 1807 and ended only in the mid-1800s.

facts: Parliament passed the Abolition of the Slave Trade Act in 1807.
The Slavery Abolition Act of 1833 ended slavery in most British colonies.
The transatlantic slave trade to Brazil continued until about 1850.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The credit line shows an organized British abolition society publishing propaganda in 1788, which links the plan to the campaign that led to the 1807 ban.

items.stem: EXTRA: The voyages represented in the plan of the Brookes were part of an Atlantic trade system in which

options.text: Enslaved Africans were shipped mainly eastward across the Indian Ocean to work on plantations in Mughal India
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Brookes was an Atlantic ship. Most captives in this trade were sent west to the Americas, not to South Asia.

options.text: European traders exchanged goods such as guns and cloth with African sellers for captives
options.label: key
options.why: European ships usually bought captives from African states and merchants on the coast and paid in manufactured goods, textiles and firearms.

options.text: African rulers were barred from trading and refused any involvement in selling captives to foreign merchants
options.label: reversal
options.why: Many African rulers and merchants, such as those of Dahomey, took an active part in selling captives to Europeans.

options.text: European armies conquered most of the West and Central African interior in order to seize laborers directly
options.label: overstated
options.why: Before the late 1800s, Europeans held mostly coastal forts and trading posts. African states controlled the interior and the supply of captives.

facts: In the 1700s, African states such as Dahomey and Asante sold captives to European traders in exchange for goods including firearms and textiles.
European slave-trading forts were concentrated on the West African coast during this period.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The plan shows a British ship carrying African captives, which ties it to the coastal exchange system of the Atlantic trade.
design.evidence_quote: STOWAGE OF 292 SLAVES

items.stem: EXTRA: Which of the following is a limitation of the plan as evidence about the experience of captives during the Middle Passage?

options.text: It was produced by slave traders who wished to hide how crowded their ships actually were from the public
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Opponents of the trade made the plan in order to expose the crowding, not to hide it.

options.text: It shows only voyages to Spanish colonies, so it cannot reveal anything about British ship conditions
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The title and context line identify the Brookes as a British ship regulated by a British law.

options.text: It was made by British opponents of the trade and does not record captives' own accounts
options.label: key
options.why: The plan comes from an abolition society and shows captives only as rows of identical figures. It cannot show how the enslaved people themselves experienced or described the voyage.

options.text: It was drawn decades after the trade ended, so its creators had no access to actual ship records
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The plan dates from 1788, while the trade was still going on, and its figures were based on the ship's legal capacity at that time.

facts: Accounts by formerly enslaved people, such as Olaudah Equiano's narrative published in 1789, give captives' own perspectives on the Middle Passage.
The Brookes plan was produced by abolitionists in 1788.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The credit line identifies abolitionists as the makers of the plan, and the image shows captives only as uniform drawn figures, not through their own voices.

spec.theme: Spanish conquistadors' encounter with the Aztec capital

sources.context: Bernal Diaz was a Spanish soldier who took part in the 1519 expedition of Hernan Cortes into Mexico; he wrote this account decades later.

items.stem: Bernal Diaz wrote this account decades after the 1519 expedition. How might that circumstance limit the usefulness of the excerpt for historians?

options.text: He wrote the account to persuade the Mexica rulers to accept Spanish authority without resisting the expedition.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Writing decades after 1519, Diaz could not have been addressing the Mexica rulers. Nothing in the source points to that audience.

options.text: Spanish royal censors required him to remove any praise of Indigenous cities and their buildings.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt openly praises the city's temples and towers, so this claim contradicts the text.

options.text: He was not present in the Valley of Mexico and relied on secondhand reports from his Indigenous allies.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The context line states he was a soldier in Cortes's expedition, and the excerpt is written as an eyewitness account ('we beheld').

options.text: His memories may have been reshaped by decades of hindsight about the outcome of the conquest.
options.label: key
options.why: The context line says he wrote decades later, as an old man. Long delay and knowledge of how the conquest ended can color what a participant recalls about a first impression.

facts: Hernan Cortes's expedition reached Tenochtitlan in November 1519.
Bernal Diaz del Castillo wrote his account decades later, around the 1560s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The credit and context lines say the account was written about 1568, decades after 1519, when Diaz was an old man.

items.stem: Which of the following details from the excerpt does Diaz use to support his claim that the Spaniards saw things they could not have dreamt of beforehand?

options.text: Comparing the stone temples and towers rising from the lake to castles in a chivalric romance
options.label: key
options.why: Diaz backs up his astonishment by likening the stone buildings in the lake to the 'fairy castles' of Amadis de Gaul, and he adds that some men thought it was a dream.

options.text: Reporting that Tlaxcalan allies warned that the Mexica planned to trap the Spaniards on the causeways
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt describes wonder, not warnings from allies. This detail does not appear in the passage.

options.text: Estimating the tens of thousands of traders and goods crowding the great marketplace of Tlatelolco
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Diaz describes the market elsewhere in his memoir, not in this passage about the first view from the causeway.

options.text: Listing the gold and featherwork gifts that Motecuhzoma sent to the Spaniards before they reached the lake
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Such gifts were really sent, but they do not appear in this excerpt.

facts: Amadis de Gaul was a Spanish chivalric romance widely read in early sixteenth-century Spain.
Tenochtitlan was built on islands in Lake Texcoco and linked to the mainland by causeways.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Diaz explains the Spaniards' astonishment by comparing the city to the fairy castles of Amadis de Gaul.
design.evidence_quote: all these buildings resembled the fairy castles we read of in Amadis de Gaul

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the historical context in which the Spanish expedition described in the excerpt took place?

options.text: Spanish competition with the Dutch East India Company for control of trade routes across the Atlantic
options.label: wrong_period
