options.why: The Dutch East India Company was founded in 1602, long after 1519, and it operated mainly in Asia.

options.text: Spanish expansion from Caribbean island colonies to the American mainland in search of wealth
options.label: key
options.why: Cortes sailed from Cuba in 1519. Spaniards had already settled Hispaniola and Cuba, and they were moving onto the mainland in search of gold and land.

options.text: Spain's search for a western sea route after the Ottomans had completely cut off all European trade with Asia
options.label: overstated
options.why: Ottoman power affected trade routes, but it never cut off all European trade with Asia. Also, by 1519 Spaniards were looking for wealth in the Americas themselves.

options.text: Portuguese efforts to build fortified trading posts along the coasts of the Indian Ocean and to tax Asian shipping
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This was a real development of the same years, but it was Portuguese and took place in Asia, so it does not explain a Spanish march into Mexico.

facts: Cortes's expedition sailed from Cuba in 1519.
Spain had established colonies on Hispaniola and Cuba before 1519.
The Dutch East India Company was founded in 1602.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line places the expedition of Hernan Cortes into Mexico in 1519, which fits the Spanish move from the Caribbean to the mainland.

items.stem: Which of the following most directly contributed to the Spanish conquest of the city described in the excerpt by 1521?

options.text: Spanish use of heavy siege artillery purchased from Ottoman foundries through Portuguese traders
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Ottoman cannon making was real, but the Spaniards did not get artillery from Ottoman foundries. Their guns were few and were not the main reason they won.

options.text: The Mexica rulers' voluntary conversion to Christianity and peaceful surrender of the city
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Mexica fought back, drove the Spaniards out in 1520, and resisted a long siege in 1521. The city did not surrender peacefully.

options.text: Alliances with Indigenous enemies of the Mexica, along with a smallpox epidemic
options.label: key
options.why: Tens of thousands of Indigenous allies, especially Tlaxcalans, fought alongside a few hundred Spaniards, and a smallpox epidemic in 1520 badly weakened the city's defenders.

options.text: The arrival of a large army of royal troops sent directly from Castile to support Cortes
options.label: overstated
options.why: Cortes led only a few hundred Spaniards and relied heavily on Indigenous allies. No large royal army was sent from Castile.

facts: Tenochtitlan fell to Spanish and Indigenous allied forces in 1521.
A smallpox epidemic struck Tenochtitlan in 1520.
Tlaxcala allied with Cortes against the Mexica.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt shows the Spaniards' first sight of the city in 1519. Students connect that encounter to the factors behind the city's fall two years later.
design.evidence_quote: the level causeway which ran in a straight line into Mexico

items.stem: Diaz's comparison of the city to the castles in Amadis de Gaul most likely served which purpose?

options.text: To argue that the city was only imaginary and that reports of its size had been greatly exaggerated
options.label: reversal
options.why: Diaz insists the city was real and that his strong language is justified. The dream image conveys amazement, not doubt that the city existed.

options.text: To prove to church officials that the Mexica practiced sorcery
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt praises the buildings' stone construction and makes no accusation of sorcery. Nothing indicates church officials were his audience.

options.text: To show that the Mexica builders had copied the castle designs brought over earlier by Spanish settlers
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Tenochtitlan was built long before any Spaniard arrived. The comparison expresses wonder and makes no claim about where the designs came from.

options.text: To help Spanish readers picture the city's grandeur through a familiar literary image
options.label: key
options.why: Diaz speaks directly to 'the reader' and uses a romance that Spaniards widely read, so he is turning an unfamiliar sight into something his readers can picture.

facts: Amadis de Gaul was a popular Spanish chivalric romance, printed in 1508.
Tenochtitlan was founded by the Mexica in the fourteenth century, long before Spanish contact.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Diaz addresses 'the reader' directly and uses a familiar romance to describe what he calls unimaginable.
design.evidence_quote: the reader must not feel surprised at the manner in which I have expressed myself

items.stem: The city Diaz describes was the capital of a state that maintained its power in central Mexico mainly by doing which of the following?

options.text: Collecting tribute from conquered city-states throughout the region
options.label: key
options.why: The Mexica-led Triple Alliance ruled through tribute. Conquered city-states sent goods such as cloth, food, and feathers, which helped pay for the grand capital Diaz describes.

options.text: Enforcing a single monotheistic faith on all subject peoples
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Mexica religion was polytheistic, and the 'temples' Diaz mentions were built for many gods. Conquered peoples also kept their own deities.

options.text: Controlling long-distance seaborne trade between the Caribbean islands and West Africa
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Mexica were a land-based power. They had no seaborne trade with West Africa, and that kind of Atlantic trade began only after European contact.

options.text: Governing provinces through the mit'a labor system and records kept on knotted quipu cords
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Mit'a labor and quipu records belonged to the Inca state in the Andes, not to the Mexica.

facts: The Mexica-led Triple Alliance collected tribute from conquered city-states in central Mexico in the fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries.
The mit'a labor system and quipu records were features of the Inca Empire.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The splendid stone temples, towers, and houses of the capital in the excerpt point to the wealth of the Mexica tribute empire.
design.evidence_quote: so high, majestic, and splendid did the temples, towers, and houses of the town

spec.theme: Rights claims in the French Revolution era: citizens and women

sources.context: The French National Assembly adopted this declaration in August 1789, soon after the French Revolution began.
Mary Wollstonecraft, an English writer, published this book in 1792, soon after the French Revolution began.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a similarity and a difference between the ideas in Source A and Source B?

options.text: Both reject the authority of written law, holding that individual reason alone should govern each person's conduct
options.label: reversal
options.why: Source A says the limits on liberty 'can only be determined by law' and calls law the expression of the general will.

options.text: Both apply Enlightenment ideas of reason and natural rights, but Source B extends them to women's lives
options.label: key
options.why: Source A grounds rights in nature and the general will. Source B wants women to act 'by the light of their own reason' and have power 'over themselves,' which applies the same reasoning to women.

options.text: Source A defends the privileges of the clergy and nobility, while Source B accepts Rousseau's view of women's education
options.label: reversal
options.why: Source A allows social distinctions only if they serve the general good, which attacks inherited privilege. Source B quotes Rousseau in order to turn his point against him.

options.text: Source A restricts rights to property-owning men, while Source B urges women to seek political power over men in society
options.label: reversal
options.why: Source A names property as a right but sets no property test in these articles. Wollstonecraft says outright, 'I do not wish them to have power over men.'

facts: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen was adopted by the French National Assembly in August 1789.
Mary Wollstonecraft published A Vindication of the Rights of Woman in 1792, criticizing Rousseau's views on educating women.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Source A states that men are born free and equal in rights, and Source B wants women to govern themselves by reason.
design.evidence_quote: discharge the important duties of life by the light of their own reason

items.stem: Which of the following developments in revolutionary France would best support Wollstonecraft's implied criticism that rights claims like those in Source A did not fully include women?

options.text: Revolutionary armies after 1792 carried ideas of liberty and national sovereignty into neighboring lands
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This describes ideas spreading abroad, not who was excluded from rights inside France.

options.text: The Civil Constitution of the Clergy of 1790 placed French priests under the authority of the state
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This is a real reform of church and state. It has nothing to do with whether women held political rights.

options.text: The Constitution of 1791 excluded women and poorer men from voting as active citizens
options.label: key
options.why: Article 6 promises every citizen a right to take part in making law, but the 1791 constitution limited voting to tax-paying adult men. That gap supports the view that women were left out.

options.text: The National Assembly abolished the feudal dues and privileges of the nobility in August 1789
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This happened, but it shows the Assembly acting on equality among men and says nothing about how women were treated.

facts: The French Constitution of 1791 divided citizens into active citizens (adult men paying a set level of tax), who could vote, and passive citizens, who could not; women could not vote.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Article 6 says every citizen may take part in making law. Evidence that women were kept out of voting backs up Source B's concern about women's rights.
design.evidence_quote: Every citizen has a right to participate personally, or through his representative, in its foundation.

items.stem: Which of the following broader developments most directly shaped the ideas expressed in both sources?

options.text: The Protestant Reformation's challenge to papal authority and the sale of indulgences in Europe
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Reformation took place in the 1500s and dealt with religious authority, not the political rights of citizens or women.

options.text: The growth of mechanized textile factories that created an urban industrial working class
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Early industrialization was underway, but neither source deals with factories or labor.

options.text: Romantic writers' celebration of emotion, national folk culture, and the beauty of untamed nature
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Romanticism stressed feeling over reason. Both sources rest their claims on reason and rights.

options.text: Enlightenment thinkers' arguments that natural rights and reason should guide society
options.label: key
options.why: Source A's natural rights and general will, and Source B's appeal to reason and its argument with Rousseau, both come out of eighteenth-century Enlightenment thought.

facts: Enlightenment thinkers such as Locke and Rousseau argued for natural rights and popular sovereignty in the 1600s and 1700s.
Rousseau's Emile (1762) set out views on women's education that Wollstonecraft criticized.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Source A's language of natural rights and the general will, and Source B's appeal to reason along with its quotation of Rousseau, both point to Enlightenment thought.
design.evidence_quote: Law is the expression of the general will.

items.stem: The principles stated in Source A most directly contributed to which of the following developments in the decade after 1789?

options.text: The Haitian Revolution, in which people in Saint-Domingue claimed equal rights and freedom
options.label: key
options.why: Beginning in 1791, free people of color and enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue drew on revolutionary claims of equal rights, and the colony went on to independence in 1804.

options.text: The Meiji Restoration, which ended the shogunate and launched rapid state-led industrialization
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Meiji Restoration began in 1868. It was a response to Western pressure, not a product of the 1789 Declaration.

options.text: The Congress of Vienna, which restored monarchies and a balance of power among European states
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Congress met in 1814 and 1815 and reacted against revolutionary principles rather than spreading them.

options.text: The Taiping Rebellion, whose leaders drew on French revolutionary writings to attack the Qing dynasty in China
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The Taiping Rebellion (1850 to 1864) came decades later. Its leader drew on his own version of Christianity, not on French revolutionary texts.

facts: The Haitian Revolution began in 1791 in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, and Haiti declared independence in 1804.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Article 1's claim that men are born free and equal gave colonial groups language they could use to demand rights.
design.evidence_quote: Men are born and remain free and equal in rights.

items.stem: EXTRA: Which of the following best describes Wollstonecraft's purpose in the excerpt from Source B?

options.text: To endorse Rousseau's claim that women should be educated mainly to please men
options.label: reversal
options.why: She quotes Rousseau so that she can turn his warning into her own goal, which rejects his view of women's education.

options.text: To argue that educating women in reason would let them govern their own lives
options.label: key
options.why: She wants women educated so that they can use 'their own reason' and have power 'over themselves.'

options.text: To call on British radicals to overthrow the monarchy and set up a republic like France
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt is about women's education and self-government. It does not call for overthrowing the British monarchy.

options.text: To urge women to seek political control over men through equal schooling and voting
options.label: reversal
options.why: She explicitly says she does not want women to have power over men, and the excerpt does not mention voting.

facts: Wollstonecraft's A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792) argued that women should receive a rational education comparable to men's.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Wollstonecraft's closing lines state her aim directly.
design.evidence_quote: I do not wish them to have power over men; but over themselves.

items.stem: EXTRA: Which of the following describes a limitation of Source A as evidence of how rights were actually extended in France after 1789?

options.text: It addresses only colonial subjects, so it reveals little about rights within France itself
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The articles speak of men, citizens and the nation in general and do not mention colonies at all.

options.text: It was drafted decades after the Revolution, so it reflects later Napoleonic legal codes
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: It is dated August 1789, at the start of the Revolution, well before the Napoleonic Code of 1804.

options.text: It states principles the Assembly adopted, not how those principles were applied
options.label: key
options.why: The Declaration sets out general principles. It cannot show by itself who actually voted or enjoyed rights in practice, and that depended on later laws such as the 1791 constitution.

options.text: It was written by royal officials who opposed the Revolution and wished to discredit it
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The credit line shows that the revolutionary National Assembly adopted it, not royal officials opposed to the Revolution.

facts: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789) stated general principles, while later laws such as the Constitution of 1791 decided who could vote.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line and the general wording of the articles show that this is a statement of principles adopted in August 1789.
design.evidence_quote: The aim of all political association is the preservation of the natural and imprescriptible rights of man.

spec.theme: The industrial revolution in Britain as seen in the 20th century

sources.context: H. G. Wells was an English writer who published a popular history of the world in 1920 for general readers.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes Wells's main claim about how the shift to factory production affected the people who made goods?

options.text: It strengthened the town guilds, which used new machinery to protect the status of skilled artisans.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Wells argues the reverse: the machine and the employer replaced the craftsman's skill and his middle-class position in the town.

options.text: It mattered mainly for the iron trade, since textile work stayed in rural households under putting-out.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Wells says cotton and then wool were among the first industries to move into factory production.

options.text: It raised most former craftsmen into the wealthy classes by giving them ownership of machines.
options.label: overstated
options.why: Wells says only some craftsmen became employers. The rest sank to the level of laborers, so this option overstates the upward path.

options.text: It divided former craftsmen into a few rising employers and many unskilled laborers.
options.label: key
options.why: Wells says the craftsman either became an employer who grew toward wealth or stayed a worker and sank to the level of a mere laborer.

facts: During British industrialization (c. 1760-1850), factory production undercut many skilled handicraft workers, such as handloom weavers.
Industrialization produced a class of factory owners and a growing class of wage laborers.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The last sentence lays out two paths for the former craftsman: becoming an employer or sinking to a laborer.
design.evidence_quote: he either became an employer of his fellows, and grew towards wealth

items.stem: The move of the iron industry to the coal districts described in the excerpt is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.text: Britain's plentiful, accessible coal deposits, which favored early industrialization there
options.label: key
options.why: Once coke made from coal replaced charcoal, ironworks moved near coalfields. Britain's large, accessible coal and iron deposits are a standard reason why industrialization began there.

options.text: The spread of railways across continental Europe, which created demand for British iron before 1750
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Steam railways first appeared in the 1820s and 1830s, so they could not have driven demand before 1750.

options.text: The exhaustion of Britain's coal reserves, which forced ironmasters to rely on imported charcoal
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt describes iron smelting moving from charcoal to coke made from coal, which is the opposite of this option.

options.text: The British government's nationalization of coal mines and ironworks to supply the Royal Navy's wars
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Britain nationalized its coal industry in 1947, long after the period described. Early ironworks and mines were privately owned.

facts: Abraham Darby began smelting iron with coke at Coalbrookdale in 1709.
Britain's large coal and iron ore deposits are widely cited as a factor in its early industrialization in the 18th century.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Wells says iron smelting turned to coke made from coal and that the industry moved from wooded counties to the coal districts.
design.evidence_quote: The iron industry shifted from the wooded country of Sussex and Surrey to the coal districts.

items.stem: The early growth of British cotton factory production described in the excerpt depended most directly on which of the following?

options.text: Domestic cotton plantations in southern England worked by tenant farmers after enclosure
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Cotton cannot be grown commercially in Britain's climate. Enclosure changed British farming, but it did not create cotton plantations.

options.text: Raw cotton imports, much of it grown by enslaved workers in the Americas
options.label: key
options.why: Britain could not grow cotton itself. Its mills relied on imported raw cotton, and by the early 1800s much of it came from enslaved labor in the United States South and the Caribbean.

options.text: Protective tariffs that the Mughal Empire placed on Indian cloth to keep it out of British markets
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Britain, not the Mughal Empire, restricted imports of Indian cotton cloth to protect its own producers.

options.text: Silk and porcelain imports from Qing China, which British factories processed into finished goods
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Britain did import Chinese goods, mainly tea, but silk and porcelain were not the raw materials that supplied cotton mills.

facts: Britain imported nearly all its raw cotton, and by the early 1800s the United States South, using enslaved labor, was its largest supplier.
Eli Whitney's cotton gin (1793) expanded cotton production in the American South.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Wells names cotton as one of the first industries to move into factory production, which ties the passage to the global supply of raw cotton.
design.evidence_quote: The cotton industry was one of the first to pass into factory production

items.stem: The fall of many workers to 'the level of a mere labourer,' as Wells describes it, most directly contributed to which of the following nineteenth-century developments in Britain?

options.text: The end of child labor in British mills as soon as steam engines replaced water wheels
options.label: reversal
options.why: Child labor continued in steam-powered mills. Parliament only limited it gradually, beginning with laws such as the Factory Act of 1833.

options.text: The abolition of the British monarchy and the creation of a workers' republic in London
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Britain kept its monarchy throughout the century. Workers pursued reform through Chartism and unions, not a successful revolution.

options.text: The formation of labor unions seeking better wages and conditions
options.label: key
options.why: As skilled workers lost status and became wage laborers, British workers organized unions, especially after the Combination Acts were repealed in 1824 and 1825.

options.text: The revival of craft guilds as the main legal regulators of wages and prices in British manufacturing
options.label: reversal
options.why: Guilds lost influence as factory production grew. They did not come back as regulators of industry.

facts: Britain repealed the Combination Acts, which had banned workers' associations, in 1824-1825.
The Factory Act of 1833 limited child labor in British textile mills.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Wells describes workers who lost their skilled status and became mere laborers, which led to organized labor responses.
design.evidence_quote: he remained a worker and sank very rapidly to the level of a mere labourer

items.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of using the excerpt as evidence of how British factory workers themselves experienced industrialization?

options.text: It describes only the cotton industry and says nothing about iron, coal, or steam power
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt discusses wool, iron, coal, coke, and steam power as well as cotton.

options.text: It was written before steam power was used in factories, so it predicts changes that had not happened
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The excerpt dates from 1920, more than a century after steam-powered factories had spread in Britain.

options.text: It was produced by mill owners who wanted to hide the dangers of factory work from Parliament
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The author was the English writer H. G. Wells, writing a popular history in 1920, not a group of mill owners.

options.text: It is a general summary written long after the events, not a worker's account
options.label: key
options.why: The credit and context lines show this is a popular world history written in 1920 for general readers. It sums up the changes from a distance rather than recording what workers themselves said.

facts: Steam-powered factories were widespread in Britain by the early 19th century, well before 1920.
H. G. Wells published The Outline of History in 1920 as a popular history for general readers.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The credit line (1920) and the context line (a popular world history for general readers) show the excerpt is a later summary, not a firsthand account by a worker.

spec.theme: The opening of Japan and the unequal exchange of privileges

sources.context: In 1854 a United States naval squadron under Commodore Matthew Perry and Japanese commissioners signed this treaty.

items.stem: The third paragraph of the excerpt (Article IX) is best understood as an example of which kind of arrangement?

options.text: A one-sided guarantee that any concession Japan later gave other powers would also go to the United States
options.label: key
options.why: Article IX is a most-favored-nation clause, and it binds only Japan. Any privilege Japan grants another nation passes automatically to the United States, which makes it a typical feature of nineteenth-century unequal treaties.

options.text: A grant of extraterritorial rights placing American citizens in Japan under the jurisdiction of United States consular courts
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Extraterritoriality came with the 1858 Harris Treaty. Article IX says nothing about courts or legal jurisdiction.

options.text: A mercantilist arrangement giving the United States exclusive trading rights in Japan and barring all other foreign nations
options.label: overstated
options.why: The clause assumes Japan may grant privileges to other nations. It secures equal treatment for the United States, not a monopoly.

options.text: A reciprocal pledge that both countries would give each other's merchants equal tariff treatment in their home ports
options.label: reversal
options.why: The clause runs in one direction only. Japan owes the United States new privileges, and nothing is promised to Japan in return.

facts: The Treaty of Kanagawa (1854) contained a most-favored-nation clause binding only Japan.
The 1858 Treaty of Amity and Commerce (Harris Treaty) added extraterritoriality and opened more ports.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Article IX requires Japan to extend to the United States any privileges it later grants other nations, and it gives Japan no matching right.
design.evidence_quote: these same privileges and advantages shall be granted likewise to the United States and to the citizens thereof without any consultation or delay

items.stem: The provision opening Simoda and Hakodadi to American ships most likely reflected which purpose of the United States negotiators?

options.text: Spreading Protestant Christianity through mission stations, reversing the Tokugawa bans imposed in the seventeenth century
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The Tokugawa bans on Christianity were real, but the article mentions only provisions and coal for ships, not missions.

options.text: Securing ports where American steamships and whalers in the Pacific could obtain coal and supplies
options.label: key
options.why: The article lists wood, water, provisions and coal. These were the needs of American whalers and of steam-powered ships crossing the Pacific toward China, which needed coaling stops.

options.text: Gaining access to Japanese silver to pay for tea and silk imports, replacing the earlier Manila galleon trade
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The galleon trade belonged to an earlier era and ran through Spanish Manila. The article is about supplying ships, not obtaining silver.

options.text: Establishing settler colonies in northern Japan for American migrants seeking land beyond the western frontier
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The ports were for receiving ships, not for settling Americans. The treaty grants no land.

facts: Perry's squadron arrived in Edo Bay in 1853 and returned in 1854.
The Treaty of Kanagawa (1854) opened Shimoda and Hakodate to American ships for supplies.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Article II lists coal and provisions as what American ships would receive at the two ports, which points to supplying ships rather than trade or settlement.
design.evidence_quote: where they can be supplied with wood, water, provisions and coal

items.stem: The treaty in the excerpt is best understood in the context of which broader process of the mid-nineteenth century?

options.text: Latin American states winning independence from Spain and Portugal and then seeking recognition through trade treaties
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Latin American independence was a real development, but it has no connection to the American naval pressure on Japan.

options.text: Japan building an overseas empire by seizing Taiwan and Korea after defeating its neighbors in a series of wars
options.label: reversal
options.why: Japan took Taiwan in 1895 and Korea in 1910. In 1854 Japan was the state receiving foreign demands, not the one expanding.

options.text: Industrialized Western states using naval power to force East Asian states into treaty relations
options.label: key
options.why: Perry's naval squadron, mentioned in the context line, pushed Japan into a treaty. In the same period Britain and other powers had used gunboats to force China into treaties after the Opium War.

options.text: European states partitioning Africa into colonies under the rules set at the Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Berlin Conference came three decades later and dealt with Africa, not East Asia.

facts: China signed the Treaty of Nanjing (1842) after the First Opium War.
Japan acquired Taiwan in 1895 and annexed Korea in 1910.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line says the treaty was signed with a United States naval squadron, which links it to Western naval pressure in East Asia.

items.stem: Which of the following was most similar to the arrangements in the excerpt?

options.text: The Zollverein customs union that lowered internal tariffs among German states before unification
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Zollverein was a trade arrangement, but it was voluntary and made among German states. It was not an unequal concession to an outside power.

options.text: The Haitian Revolution's abolition of slavery and creation of an independent state in the Caribbean
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Haitian Revolution was an anticolonial revolt. It does not resemble a treaty opening ports to a foreign power.

options.text: The Ottoman Tanzimat decrees that reorganized imperial law and granted equality to non-Muslim subjects
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Tanzimat decrees were internal reforms by the Ottoman state. They were not port concessions forced by an outside power.

options.text: The treaties that opened Chinese ports to Western traders after the First Opium War
options.label: key
options.why: China's treaties of the 1840s opened ports to foreigners and included most-favored-nation guarantees for Western powers. These are the same features found in the Kanagawa treaty.

facts: The Treaty of Nanjing (1842) opened five Chinese ports to British trade.
The 1843 supplementary Treaty of the Bogue gave Britain most-favored-nation treatment in China.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Port openings for foreign ships in Article II and the one-sided privilege clause in Article IX match the Chinese treaty-port system.
design.evidence_quote: are granted by the Japanese as ports for he reception for American ships

items.stem: The concessions in the excerpt, along with later treaties of the same kind, most directly contributed to which development in Japan?

options.text: The overthrow of the Tokugawa shogunate and a state-led drive to industrialize under Meiji rule
options.label: key
options.why: Anger at the unequal treaties weakened the shogunate, which fell in 1868. Meiji leaders then pursued Western-style industry and military reform, partly so they could revise the treaties.

options.text: The division of Japan into British and American spheres of influence controlling its major railways and mines
options.label: overstated
options.why: Japan stayed independent and built its own railways. Foreign spheres of influence were a feature of late Qing China.

options.text: A massive peasant rebellion led by a Christian convert that devastated southern China for over a decade
options.label: misattributed
options.why: This describes the Taiping Rebellion in China (1850 to 1864), not a development in Japan.

options.text: A return to strict seclusion after Japanese forces expelled all foreign traders from Nagasaki in the 1860s
options.label: reversal
options.why: Japan did not go back into seclusion. After 1868 it expanded contact with the West.

facts: The Meiji Restoration of 1868 ended the Tokugawa shogunate.
The Meiji government promoted state-sponsored industrialization and sought to revise the unequal treaties, finishing the revisions by 1911.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The one-sided privileges in Article IX show the kind of unequal terms that Japanese reformers later blamed on the shogunate.
design.evidence_quote: if, at any future day, the government of Japan shall grant to any other nation or nations privileges and advantages

items.stem: The opening article's promise of a perfect, permanent and universal peace is limited as evidence of the relationship between the two countries for which reason?

options.text: It was inserted after the Meiji Restoration, when the new government rewrote every treaty signed by the shogunate
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The treaty is dated 1854, before the Meiji Restoration. Treaty revision was negotiated from the 1890s, not done by rewriting old texts.

options.text: It presents formal goodwill but omits the naval pressure under which Japanese officials agreed to sign
options.label: key
options.why: The context line notes the treaty was made with a United States naval squadron present. The friendly language of the first article hides the coercion behind it.

options.text: It describes a defensive alliance that the two countries later invoked together against Russian expansion in the Pacific
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The article promises peace, not an alliance. Japan's alliance against Russia was the 1902 Anglo-Japanese Alliance with Britain.

options.text: It was drafted by Japanese commissioners who wanted to conceal their plans for attacking American ships in Edo Bay
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Neither the text nor the credit line suggests any Japanese plan to attack. The shogunate chose to negotiate.

facts: Perry's 1853 and 1854 visits to Japan were made with armed naval squadrons.
The Anglo-Japanese Alliance was signed in 1902.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line's mention of a naval squadron, set against the article's language of sincere amity, shows the gap between the treaty's wording and the conditions in which it was signed.
design.evidence_quote: There shall be a perfect, permanent and universal peace, and a sincere and cordial amity

spec.theme: Imperial rivalry over China in the late 1890s

sources.context: This cartoon appeared in a French newspaper supplement in January 1898, after several European powers and Japan had gained special rights in parts of China.

items.stem: The cartoonist's depiction of the Chinese official standing behind the table most likely reflects which of the following?

options.text: Chinese nationalist demands to overthrow the Manchu dynasty and establish a republic modeled on the West
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The cartoon is a French work for a French audience. It does not express the views of Chinese revolutionaries.

options.text: European admiration for Confucian scholar-officials as models of rational government
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Some Enlightenment writers in the 1700s admired Chinese government, but this mocking caricature from 1898 shows nothing of that admiration.

options.text: European views of the Qing state as weak and unable to stop foreign encroachment
options.label: key
options.why: The official is drawn as a caricature raising his hands in alarm while foreign figures cut up the cake labeled CHINE. That matches a common European view of the 1890s, after defeats in the Opium Wars and the war with Japan, that the Qing could not defend China.

options.text: French approval of Qing efforts to modernize the army and build arsenals under the Self-Strengthening Movement
options.label: reversal
options.why: The cartoon shows China as helpless. It does not praise Chinese modernization.

facts: Qing China lost the Opium Wars (1839-1842 and 1856-1860) to Britain and France.
China was defeated by Japan in the Sino-Japanese War of 1894-1895.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The Chinese official is caricatured with raised hands and an alarmed face while foreign rulers cut the cake, which suggests the cartoonist saw China as helpless.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the main claim made by the cartoon?

options.text: The great powers had agreed to share equal trading rights across all of China under a common treaty
options.label: reversal
options.why: The cartoon stresses rivalry, with each power grabbing its own slice. It does not show cooperation or equal access.

options.text: Japan was leading a united Asian resistance to protect China from further Western economic expansion
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Japan sits at the table among the powers dividing the cake. It is not shown defending China.

options.text: China had been fully conquered and placed under the direct rule of a single European colonial government
options.label: overstated
options.why: The cartoon shows several powers taking slices, and the Qing still governed China. It does not show one power ruling the whole country.

options.text: China was being carved up by rival powers competing for territory and influence
options.label: key
options.why: Several rulers hold knives over a cake labeled CHINE, and slices are already marked Kiao-Tcheou and Port-Arthur. The image claims that China was being divided among competing powers.

facts: Germany seized Jiaozhou Bay (Kiaochow) in November 1897 and obtained a lease in 1898.
Russia occupied Port Arthur in December 1897 and obtained a lease in 1898.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The cake labeled CHINE, the slices marked with Chinese ports, and the knives held by several rulers show China being divided among rivals.
design.evidence_quote: Le gateau des Rois et... des Empereurs

items.stem: The competition depicted in the cartoon is best understood as part of which broader process of the late nineteenth century?

options.text: Industrial states seeking markets, raw materials, and strategic ports overseas
options.label: key
options.why: The scramble for leased ports and spheres of influence in China in the 1890s was part of the New Imperialism, in which industrialized states competed abroad, as they also did in the partition of Africa.

options.text: Chartered joint-stock companies such as the Dutch East India Company founding coastal trading posts
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Chartered companies of this kind belong mainly to the 1600s and 1700s. In 1898 states acted directly, as the rulers at the table show.

options.text: Ottoman Tanzimat reforms reorganizing the legal system and the army along European lines
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Tanzimat reforms were real nineteenth-century reforms, but they were a response by the Ottoman state, not the imperial competition over China shown here.

options.text: Atlantic revolutionary movements spreading ideas of popular sovereignty and natural rights to Asia
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Atlantic Revolutions were political upheavals of about 1750 to 1830. They do not explain great-power competition for Chinese ports.

facts: The Berlin Conference of 1884-1885 set rules for European claims in Africa during the New Imperialism.
In 1897-1898 Germany, Russia, Britain and France gained leased territories or spheres of influence in China.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Rulers of several industrial powers each claim slices named after Chinese ports, which fits the wider pattern of imperial competition for strategic and commercial footholds.
design.evidence_quote: PORT-ARTHUR

items.stem: The foreign encroachment shown in the cartoon most directly contributed to which of the following developments in China within the next few years?

options.text: The Meiji Restoration's abolition of the samurai class and creation of a conscript army
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Meiji reforms took place in Japan from the 1868 Restoration onward. They did not result from the division of China in 1898.

options.text: The Boxer Rebellion's attacks on foreigners and Chinese Christians
options.label: key
options.why: Anger at foreign concessions and missionary activity, especially in Shandong where Germany took Jiaozhou, fed the Boxer uprising of 1899 to 1901.

options.text: The First Opium War, which ended with Britain gaining Hong Kong in the Treaty of Nanjing
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The First Opium War ended in 1842. It was an earlier cause of foreign influence in China, not a result of the 1898 situation.

options.text: The Taiping Rebellion's attempt to found a Heavenly Kingdom under Hong Xiuquan
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Taiping Rebellion took place from 1850 to 1864, decades before the scramble for concessions of 1897 and 1898.

facts: The Boxer Rebellion (1899-1901) targeted foreigners and Chinese Christians and was put down by an eight-nation foreign force.
The Boxer movement began in Shandong province, where Germany had gained Jiaozhou Bay in 1898.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The Kiao-Tcheou slice points to German expansion in Shandong, where resentment of foreign intrusion later fed the Boxer movement.
design.evidence_quote: KIAO-TCHEOU

items.stem: Which of the following developments best explains why a figure representing Japan is included among the powers at the table?

options.text: Japan's defeat of Russia in 1905, which made it the leading power in Manchuria
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Russo-Japanese War came seven years after this cartoon was published, so it cannot explain Japan's place in it.

options.text: Japan's role as the chief supplier of opium smuggled into southern Chinese ports
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Opium smuggled into China came mainly from British India by way of British traders, not from Japan.

options.text: Japan's victory over China in the Sino-Japanese War of 1894 to 1895
options.label: key
options.why: Japan defeated China and gained Taiwan in the Treaty of Shimonoseki in 1895. This made Japan an imperial competitor in China alongside the Western powers.

options.text: Japan's Tokugawa policy restricting European traders to the Dutch at Nagasaki
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Tokugawa restrictions limited foreign contact before the 1850s. They do not explain why Japan was an imperial power in 1898.

facts: Japan defeated China in the Sino-Japanese War of 1894-1895.
By the Treaty of Shimonoseki (1895) China ceded Taiwan to Japan.

design.key_evidence_in_source: A figure in Japanese dress, with a sword beside him, sits among the European rulers at the China cake, which shows Japan as one of the imperial competitors.

items.stem: Because the cartoon appeared in a popular French newspaper, it would be most useful to a historian studying which of the following?

options.text: The relative size and readiness of the Qing armies and navy at the start of 1898
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The cartoon gives no military data. Its caricature shows attitudes, not measurable strength.

options.text: How Chinese peasants in Shandong experienced the arrival of foreign railways and missions
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The cartoon is a French view and shows no Chinese commoners' experience. This is the limit of its perspective.

options.text: The exact terms of the leases the Qing government granted to Germany and Russia
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: A cartoon names places but gives no treaty terms. The historian would need the treaty texts for that.

options.text: How European audiences viewed the competition for influence in China
options.label: key
options.why: A cartoon in a mass-circulation French paper shows how the scramble for China was presented to European readers. This is the strength of its point of view, and it is also its limit.

facts: Le Petit Journal was a mass-circulation Paris daily newspaper in the late nineteenth century.
Germany and Russia obtained leases of Jiaozhou Bay and Port Arthur from the Qing in 1898.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The credit line identifies the source as a cartoon in a French newspaper supplement, so it shows European opinion rather than Chinese experience or official terms.

spec.theme: Revolution and the army in Russia in 1917

sources.context: This order was issued in March 1917 by the Petrograd Soviet, a council of workers' and soldiers' deputies, a few days after Tsar Nicholas II gave up the throne.

items.stem: Point 4 of the order, which limits obedience to the State Duma's military commission, best illustrates which of the following features of Russian politics in 1917?

options.text: A division of authority between the Soviet and the Duma-based Provisional Government
options.label: key
options.why: Point 4 says Duma orders are to be obeyed only when they do not contradict the Soviet. That shows the dual power that arose after the tsar fell, when the Provisional Government formed from the Duma shared authority with the Petrograd Soviet.

options.text: The tsar's reliance on the elected Duma to approve military commands after the 1905 revolution
options.label: misattributed
options.why: After 1905 the tsar kept control of the army, and the Duma never approved military commands. The order is also a Soviet document, not a tsarist one.

options.text: The restoration of officer control over the army by the imperial general staff
options.label: reversal
options.why: The order takes power away from officers by giving soldiers' committees control of weapons. It does not restore officer authority.

options.text: The Bolshevik consolidation of one-party rule through the Cheka and the banning of rival parties
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Bolsheviks built one-party rule only after they took power in late 1917 and during the civil war. In March 1917 the Soviet was a multiparty council that was competing with the Duma.

facts: After the February Revolution of 1917, the Provisional Government, formed from Duma leaders, and the Petrograd Soviet shared power, a situation called dual power.
Nicholas II abdicated in March 1917.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Point 4 makes the Duma commission's orders conditional on agreement with the Soviet, which shows two rival centers of authority.
design.evidence_quote: The orders of the military commission of the State Duma are to be fulfilled only in those cases which do not contradict the orders

items.stem: Based on its provisions, the Petrograd Soviet most likely issued the order for which of the following purposes?

options.text: To place the army under the full command of the Provisional Government's ministers
options.label: reversal
options.why: The order actually limits obedience to the Duma's military commission and puts the Soviet's decisions first.

options.text: To bind soldiers to the Soviet so officers could not turn troops against it
options.label: key
options.why: The order puts weapons under soldiers' committees, forbids handing them to officers, and makes Soviet decisions the final authority. These measures would keep the garrison loyal to the Soviet and stop officers from using troops against the revolution.

options.text: To announce Russia's withdrawal from the war and the opening of peace talks with Germany
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Russia left the war under Bolshevik rule with the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk in 1918. The order does not mention peace talks.

options.text: To persuade soldiers to leave the front lines and return home to seize the estates of nobles
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The order requires the strictest discipline in service and says nothing about deserting or seizing land. Some soldiers later did both, but this document does not call for it.

facts: The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, signed in March 1918, took Russia out of World War I.
Soldiers of the Petrograd garrison joined the protests that brought down the tsarist government in early 1917.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Point 5 keeps weapons under committee control and away from officers, and point 4 puts Soviet decisions above Duma orders.
design.evidence_quote: are not in any case to be given out to officers, even upon their command

items.stem: Which of the following broader conditions most directly explains why soldiers in Petrograd in 1917 were receptive to the measures in Order No. 1?

options.text: Mass unemployment during the Great Depression, which turned soldiers against the officer corps
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Great Depression started in 1929, more than ten years after this order.

options.text: Balkan nationalist movements that drew Russia into war to protect Serbia from Austria-Hungary
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This explains why Russia entered the war in 1914. It does not explain why soldiers were disaffected by 1917.

options.text: Wartime defeats and shortages that eroded loyalty to the tsarist state among troops
options.label: key
options.why: Heavy losses in the First World War and food shortages in the cities turned many soldiers and workers against the old order. The Petrograd garrison joined the uprising, and that made soldiers open to committees and new civil rights.

options.text: Russia's defeat by Japan in 1904-1905, which led the tsar to grant the October Manifesto
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Russo-Japanese War helped cause the 1905 revolution. The immediate setting of the 1917 order was the strain of the First World War.

facts: Russia suffered heavy military losses in World War I between 1914 and 1917.
Food shortages and strikes in Petrograd helped spark the February Revolution of 1917.
Russia mobilized in 1914 in support of Serbia against Austria-Hungary.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The order is addressed to the garrison and the fleet in wartime and gives soldiers committees and civil rights, which reflects troops who had broken with the old command structure.
design.evidence_quote: To all the soldiers of the Guard, army, artillery and fleet for immediate and precise execution

items.stem: The weakening of officers' authority reflected in points 5 and 6 of the order most likely contributed to which later development?

options.text: Stalin's purge of the Red Army officer corps in the late 1930s
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The purges came two decades later and grew out of Stalin's terror, not out of this 1917 order.

options.text: The restoration of the Romanov dynasty as a constitutional monarchy backed by the army
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Romanov monarchy was never restored. The order moved power toward soldiers' committees, not toward the dynasty.

options.text: The Provisional Government's success in crushing the Bolsheviks and holding power through 1918
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Bolsheviks overthrew the Provisional Government in late 1917.

options.text: The decline of the army's fighting capacity before Russia left the war in 1918
options.label: key
options.why: Soldiers' committees controlled weapons and officers lost authority, which undermined command. Russia's army fell apart over 1917, and the Bolsheviks took Russia out of the war in 1918.

facts: The Bolsheviks seized power from the Provisional Government in October (Old Style) 1917.
The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk ended Russia's participation in World War I in March 1918.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Point 5 takes control of weapons away from officers, and point 6 abolishes compulsory saluting outside service. Both weakened the command hierarchy.
design.evidence_quote: Standing at attention and compulsory saluting outside of service are especially abolished.

items.stem: The soldiers' committees called for in point 1 of the order were most similar to which of the following developments elsewhere at the end of the First World War?

options.text: Sailors' mutinies and soldiers' councils in Germany at the end of 1918
options.label: key
options.why: In late 1918 German sailors mutinied at Kiel, and workers' and soldiers' councils spread across Germany as the monarchy collapsed. These councils were close parallels to the elected committees in the order.

options.text: Meiji Japan's creation of a conscript army bound by oath to obey the emperor
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This was a nineteenth-century reform, and it strengthened top-down command. The order did the opposite.

options.text: Fascist squads that helped Mussolini pressure the king into naming him premier in 1922
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Blackshirts were a right-wing paramilitary force that worked against left-wing councils. They were not democratically elected soldiers' bodies.

options.text: Land redistribution promised by Mexico's 1917 constitution after years of revolution
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Mexico's land reform was a real revolutionary change from the same year, but it concerned land, not elected councils of soldiers.

facts: Sailors at Kiel mutinied in November 1918, and workers' and soldiers' councils formed across Germany.
Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicated in November 1918.
Mussolini became Italian prime minister after the March on Rome in 1922.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Point 1 orders every unit and warship to elect soldiers' and sailors' committees.
design.evidence_quote: immediately choose committees from the elected representatives of the soldiers and sailors

spec.theme: The Russian revolutionary government's appeal to workers abroad

sources.context: Vladimir Lenin, leader of the Bolshevik government of Russia, wrote this letter in August 1918, during the Russian Civil War.

items.stem: Based on the excerpt and its context, Lenin's main purpose in writing the letter was most likely to

options.text: recruit American volunteers to travel to Russia and fight alongside the Red Army against the White forces
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the excerpt asks for volunteers or military help. Lenin's appeal is ideological and directed at workers in their own country.

options.text: encourage American workers to oppose their government's imperialist policies
options.label: key
options.why: Lenin addresses the American proletariat 'insofar as it is the enemy of American imperialism' and says it must 'perform an important task,' which signals a call for workers to act against their own government.

options.text: urge the British and German governments to sign a negotiated peace ending the fighting on the Western Front
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Lenin condemns both imperialist groups, the English and the German, as 'playing false.' The letter is addressed to American workers, not to either government.

options.text: persuade the United States government to recognize the Bolshevik regime and resume normal trade with Russia
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The letter goes to workers, not to the American government, and it treats that government as imperialist rather than as a partner to win over.

facts: Lenin led the Bolshevik government that took power in Russia in November 1917.
The Bolsheviks called for workers' revolutions against capitalist governments in other countries.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The opening addresses the American revolutionary proletariat as the enemy of American imperialism, a group with an important task to carry out.
design.evidence_quote: the revolutionary proletariat of America--insofar as it is the enemy of American imperialism--is destined to perform an important task

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the argument Lenin makes about the First World War in the excerpt?

options.text: American workers had already overthrown capitalism at home and should now spread their revolution to Europe
options.label: overstated
options.why: Lenin hopes American workers will take on a revolutionary task, but he does not claim they have already overthrown capitalism.

options.text: Britain had been badly weakened by the war and was forced to give up parts of its empire to its allies
options.label: reversal
options.why: Lenin argues the opposite. He says England 'has lost not a span' of land and has gained German colonies, Mesopotamia and Palestine.

options.text: Capitalist wars enrich the strongest powers at the expense of the weakest
options.label: key
options.why: Lenin points to 'the great law of capitalism in all wars': the richest and mightiest profit most while the weakest are exploited. He uses Britain's gains as his example.

options.text: Germany lost the war mainly because it lacked colonial possessions and overseas raw materials
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Lenin mentions that Britain took Germany's colonies, but he never says that a shortage of colonies caused Germany's defeat.

facts: Marxist-Leninist thought held that imperialism was a stage of capitalism and that imperialist rivalry caused the First World War.
Lenin presented the war of 1914-1918 as an imperialist war among capitalist powers.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Lenin states a general 'law of capitalism in all wars' and then backs it up with Britain's territorial gains.
design.evidence_quote: he who is richest and mightiest profits the most, takes the greatest share of the spoils while he who is weakest is exploited

items.stem: After the war, British control over the territories that Lenin says Britain gained was most directly made formal through

options.text: the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, under which Russia gave up Poland, the Baltic lands, and Ukraine to Germany
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: This 1918 treaty concerned Russia's losses to the Central Powers. It did not deal with British gains in Africa or the Middle East.

options.text: the Atlantic Charter, which promised self-determination to colonial peoples once the fighting had ended
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Atlantic Charter dates from 1941, during the Second World War, and it did not formalize British control of these lands.

options.text: the Berlin Conference, which divided Africa among European powers and set rules for claiming new territory
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Berlin Conference met in 1884-1885, decades before Britain took Germany's African colonies during the First World War.

options.text: League of Nations mandates over former Ottoman and German territories
options.label: key
options.why: Under the postwar peace settlement, Britain received League of Nations mandates over Mesopotamia (Iraq), Palestine and former German colonies such as Tanganyika. These mandates put into legal form the occupation Lenin describes.

facts: British forces captured Baghdad in 1917 and Jerusalem in December 1917.
After World War I, the League of Nations mandate system assigned Britain mandates over Iraq and Palestine, along with former German territory in Africa such as Tanganyika.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt lists Britain's acquisition of German colonies in Africa and its occupation of Mesopotamia and Palestine, the lands later held as British mandates.
design.evidence_quote: it has acquired control of all German colonies in Africa, has occupied Mesopotamia and Palestine

items.stem: EXTRA. Which of the following contexts most directly explains why Lenin, writing in August 1918, treated American imperialism as an enemy of the Russian revolution?

options.text: Allied forces, including US troops, intervened in the Russian Civil War
options.label: key
options.why: In 1918 the Allies, the United States among them, sent troops to northern Russia and Siberia during the Civil War. This led Bolshevik leaders to see American power as hostile.

options.text: The Washington Naval Conference had placed strict limits on the size of the Soviet navy in the Pacific
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Washington Naval Conference met in 1921-1922, after the letter was written, and Soviet Russia was not a party to it.

options.text: American corporations had seized control of the Russian oil fields of the Caucasus soon after the revolution
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: No American seizure of Caucasus oil fields took place in this period, and the excerpt mentions nothing of the kind.

options.text: The United States had stayed out of the First World War and was profitably trading with both warring sides
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The United States entered the war in April 1917, so by August 1918 it was fighting on the Allied side and was no longer neutral.

facts: In 1918 the United States sent troops to northern Russia (Archangel) and to Siberia as part of the Allied intervention.
The Russian Civil War between the Bolsheviks and their opponents was fought from roughly 1918 to 1921.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line places the letter during the Russian Civil War, and the text calls American imperialism the enemy, which points to the Allied intervention.
design.evidence_quote: insofar as it is the enemy of American imperialism

items.stem: EXTRA. Lenin's position as Bolshevik leader most limits the usefulness of the excerpt as evidence about which of the following?

options.text: the Marxist arguments Bolsheviks used to seek support from workers in industrial countries
options.label: reversal
options.why: A letter from the Bolshevik leader to American workers is a strong example of these appeals, so his position adds to its value on this subject.

options.text: why British leaders sought control of Mesopotamia and Palestine
options.label: key
options.why: Lenin reads British motives through a Marxist theory that capitalist powers fight for spoils, and he had no inside knowledge of British decision-making. That makes the letter weak evidence of what British leaders actually intended.

options.text: which territories the Allies had occupied or claimed from the Central Powers by the end of 1918
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The territorial gains Lenin lists match the well-documented record of wartime occupation, so his ideological bias does little to weaken the source on this point.

options.text: how Bolshevik leaders interpreted the causes and results of the First World War
options.label: reversal
options.why: The letter is direct evidence of exactly this. Lenin's point of view makes it more useful on this subject, not less.

facts: Lenin was the leader of the Bolshevik Party and a Marxist theorist of imperialism.
Britain occupied Mesopotamia and Palestine during World War I, completing these conquests in 1917-1918.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Lenin explains Britain's gains through a general 'law of capitalism' rather than through evidence of British intentions, which shows how his ideology shapes his account of other governments' motives.
design.evidence_quote: The four years of war have shown in their effects the great law of capitalism in all wars

spec.theme: Indian nationalism and the critique of British rule

sources.context: Mohandas Gandhi, an Indian lawyer who had worked in South Africa, wrote this book in 1909 as a dialogue between a Reader and an Editor; the Editor states Gandhi's views.

items.stem: Which of the following best explains the purpose of the Editor's argument in the excerpt?

options.text: To urge members of the British Parliament to grant India self-governing dominion status like Canada and Australia had
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the excerpt addresses Parliament or dominion status. The 'we' of the passage refers to Indians.

options.text: To call on Indians to drive out the English through an armed uprising like the rebellion of 1857
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The passage blames Indian cooperation and calls for no violence. Gandhi's approach was nonviolent.

options.text: To convince Indians that British rule depended on their own cooperation and could be ended by withdrawing it
options.label: key
options.why: The Editor says the English stay 'because we keep them,' so ending rule depends on Indian choices. This matches Gandhi's later strategy of noncooperation.

options.text: To defend British rule in India as the natural result of the superior military strength and organization of the English
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt explicitly denies that the English are in India 'because of their strength.'

facts: Gandhi wrote Hind Swaraj in 1909 while sailing from London to South Africa.
Gandhi led the Non-Cooperation Movement in India in 1920-1922.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The Editor's claim that Indians 'keep' the English implies that Indians can stop doing so.
design.evidence_quote: They are not in India because of their strength, but because we keep them.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the Editor's claim about how British power in India developed?

options.text: Indian rulers lost power because they lacked the silver needed to match the Company's trade
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Silver appears as a temptation to Indians, not as a resource Indian rulers lacked.

options.text: Indian merchants were compelled by Company officers to purchase English goods against their own economic interests
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Editor treats Indian purchases as a voluntary choice made by people 'tempted' by silver, not as something forced on them.

options.text: The British arrived in India intending to found a kingdom and relied mainly on military conquest to do so
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt says they 'had not the slightest intention' of establishing a kingdom, and it rejects strength as the explanation.

options.text: British power in India began with trade and grew because Indians aided and dealt with the Company
options.label: key
options.why: The Editor says the English came 'for purposes of trade.' He then asks who assisted the Company's officers and bought its goods, and answers 'we did all this.'

facts: The British East India Company first came to India as a trading company in the early 1600s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The passage connects the Company's trading origins with Indians who helped its officers and bought its goods.
design.evidence_quote: They came to our country originally for purposes of trade.

items.stem: The argument in the excerpt most directly relates to which later development in the Indian independence movement between 1919 and 1947?

options.text: Mass campaigns of noncooperation and boycotts of British goods and institutions
options.label: key
options.why: The Editor says Indians sustained British rule by helping the Company and buying its goods. Gandhi's later campaigns asked Indians to stop doing exactly that, for example by boycotting British cloth and institutions.

options.text: The partition of British India into separate states of India and Pakistan in 1947 amid communal violence
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Partition did happen, but it grew out of Hindu-Muslim political division, not out of the excerpt's argument about cooperation.

options.text: The expansion of state-led heavy industry through national five-year economic plans
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Nehru's five-year plans started in 1951, after independence, and they were not a strategy for ending British rule.

options.text: The Indian National Army's armed campaign alongside Japanese forces to drive the British out
options.label: reversal
options.why: Subhas Chandra Bose's INA used armed force with Axis support. This was the opposite of the excerpt's focus on withdrawing Indian cooperation.

facts: Gandhi led the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-1922), which included boycotts of British goods, courts and schools.
Nehru's government launched India's first five-year plan in 1951.
Subhas Chandra Bose led the Indian National Army with Japanese support during the Second World War.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The rhetorical questions about who assisted the Company and who bought its goods point toward ending British rule by withdrawing that cooperation and boycotting British goods.
design.evidence_quote: Who assisted the Company's officers? Who was tempted at the sight of their silver? Who bought their goods?

items.stem: The context line notes that Gandhi had worked in South Africa. Which experience there most directly shaped the view of power in the excerpt?

options.text: Campaigning alongside Afrikaner nationalists for the independence of the Boer republics from British rule
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Gandhi did not campaign for Boer independence. In the South African War he organized an Indian ambulance corps that served on the British side.

options.text: Leading nonviolent protest by Indians against laws that discriminated against them
options.label: key
options.why: From 1906 Gandhi led satyagraha campaigns by Indians in the Transvaal against discriminatory registration laws. That experience shaped his belief that rule depends on the cooperation of the ruled.

options.text: Organizing Indian indentured laborers into a Marxist party modeled on the Bolsheviks
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Bolsheviks took power in 1917, after the book was written, and Gandhi was never a Marxist organizer.

options.text: Negotiating the end of apartheid policies with the leaders of the African National Congress
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Apartheid became official policy in 1948, and its end was negotiated in the early 1990s, long after 1909.

facts: Gandhi lived and worked in South Africa from 1893 to 1914.
Beginning in 1906 Gandhi led satyagraha against the Transvaal law requiring Asians to register.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line says Gandhi had worked in South Africa, which ties the passage to his civil resistance campaigns there.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a limitation of the excerpt as evidence for how the East India Company gained control over much of India?

options.text: It was written after independence in 1947, so the author could not have known the Company's methods
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The credit line dates the text to 1909, almost four decades before independence.

options.text: It relies on trade statistics that the Company itself compiled
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt contains no statistics. It rests its case on rhetorical questions and a general appeal to history.

options.text: Its aim of stressing Indian responsibility leads it to pass over Company warfare such as at Plassey
options.label: key
options.why: Gandhi wanted Indians to see their own role in British rule, so the passage plays down military force. Yet the Company did expand through wars, including its victory at Plassey in 1757.

options.text: It was written by a British colonial official who wished to justify Company rule to a skeptical public in London
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The credit line names Gandhi, an Indian lawyer and political leader, as the author, and the passage criticizes Indian cooperation rather than justifying the Company.

facts: The East India Company defeated the Nawab of Bengal at the Battle of Plassey in 1757.
Hind Swaraj was written in 1909.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The Editor denies that British strength explains their presence. This shows his persuasive purpose, which leaves out the military side of Company expansion.
design.evidence_quote: They are not in India because of their strength, but because we keep them.

spec.theme: The division of Berlin during the Cold War

sources.context: This photograph from the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency shows work on a wall dividing East Berlin from West Berlin in September 1961.

items.stem: Based on the credit line and the photograph, during which historical situation was the image most likely taken?

options.text: Crowds on both sides were dismantling the barrier after the East German government opened its border crossings
options.label: reversal
options.why: The photograph shows the wall being built in 1961. The crossings opened and the wall came down in 1989.

options.text: The victorious Allies were dividing the city into four occupation sectors after the defeat of Nazi Germany
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Berlin was divided into occupation sectors in 1945. The physical wall in the photograph dates from 1961.

options.text: The Soviet Union was blockading road and rail routes into West Berlin, prompting a large Western airlift of food and supplies
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Berlin Blockade and Airlift happened in 1948 and 1949, more than a decade before this 1961 photograph.

options.text: East German authorities were sealing the border between the city's sectors to stop emigration to the West
options.label: key
options.why: The September 1961 date and the scene of workers setting concrete slabs behind barbed wire match the building of the Berlin Wall, which began in August 1961 to stop East Germans from leaving for West Berlin.

facts: Construction of the Berlin Wall began on August 13, 1961.
East Germany built the wall largely to stop large numbers of its citizens from leaving through West Berlin.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The date in the credit line and the image of workers putting concrete slabs in place behind barbed wire point to the building of the wall in 1961.
design.evidence_quote: Constructing Berlin Wall (September 18, 1961)

items.stem: The construction shown in the photograph is best understood in the context of which broader development of the mid-twentieth century?

options.text: Rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union over the political future of postwar Europe
options.label: key
options.why: Berlin was split between Soviet-backed East Germany and Western-aligned West Berlin, so the wall was a product of the superpower rivalry over postwar Europe.

options.text: The spread of fascist regimes that challenged the post-First World War settlement in Europe
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Fascist regimes belong to the interwar period. By 1961 the context was the Cold War.

options.text: The founding of the Non-Aligned Movement by newly independent states seeking to stay out of superpower alliances
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Non-Aligned Movement was founded in 1961, but it was a response to bloc politics by other states. It was not the setting that produced the division of Berlin.

options.text: Nationalist movements in Africa and Asia demanding independence from British and French colonial rule
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Decolonization was happening in these same years, but it does not explain why a wall divided Berlin.

facts: After 1945 Germany and Berlin were divided between Soviet and Western zones; the two German states were founded in 1949.
The Berlin Wall stood from 1961 to 1989 as a symbol of the Cold War division of Europe.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line says the wall divided East Berlin from West Berlin, and that division reflected the split between the Soviet and Western blocs.
design.evidence_quote: a wall dividing East Berlin from West Berlin in September 1961

items.stem: The barrier shown being built in the photograph was opened in 1989. That opening was most directly related to which of the following developments?

options.text: Economic reforms in China under Deng Xiaoping that opened the country to foreign investment and markets
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Deng's reforms were real, but they took place in China and did not bring about the opening of the Berlin border.

options.text: Soviet reforms under Gorbachev and mass protests that weakened communist rule in Eastern Europe
options.label: key
options.why: Gorbachev's reforms and his unwillingness to use force to hold the Eastern bloc together, along with mass protests in East Germany and nearby states, led to the opening of the wall in November 1989.

options.text: A NATO military offensive that forced Warsaw Pact troops to withdraw from East Germany
options.label: misattributed
options.why: No NATO offensive took place. The wall opened through peaceful political change, not military defeat.

options.text: The peaceful resolution of the Cuban Missile Crisis, which led to a direct communication line between superpowers
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Cuban Missile Crisis was in 1962 and the hotline was set up in 1963. Both came decades before the wall opened.

facts: The Berlin Wall was opened on November 9, 1989.
Mikhail Gorbachev, Soviet leader from 1985, pursued the reform policies of glasnost and perestroika.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The question builds on the wall shown under construction in 1961 and asks how it relates to its opening in 1989.
design.evidence_quote: Constructing Berlin Wall

items.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of the photograph for historians studying the construction of the Berlin Wall?

options.text: It shows the wall only after completion, so it reveals nothing about how quickly construction began in 1961
options.label: reversal
