options.why: The photograph shows construction still underway in September 1961, not a finished wall.

options.text: Because it was taken at night, it cannot show that workers built the barrier using heavy concrete slabs and barbed wire
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The floodlights make the concrete slabs and the barbed wire clearly visible, even at night.

options.text: As a U.S. intelligence photograph, it does not show how East German leaders justified building the barrier
options.label: key
options.why: The image comes from a U.S. agency and shows only the physical work. It cannot tell historians how the East German government explained or defended the wall.

options.text: Because it was made by a U.S. agency, the scene must have been staged to exaggerate the size of the wall
options.label: overstated
options.why: Coming from a Cold War rival may affect what a source chooses to show, but nothing suggests the scene was staged.

facts: The East German government officially called the Berlin Wall an anti-fascist protective barrier.
The Central Intelligence Agency is a U.S. government intelligence agency.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The credit line names a U.S. intelligence agency as the creator, and the image shows only workers and materials, not East German statements.
design.evidence_quote: Central Intelligence Agency (U.S. government photograph), 1961

items.stem: Which of the following was most similar to the division of Berlin shown in the photograph?

options.text: The breakup of Austria-Hungary into several new national states after the First World War
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This happened in 1918 and 1919 and was driven by nationalism after the empire's defeat, not by Cold War rivalry.

options.text: The splitting of the Ottoman Arab provinces into British and French mandates under the League of Nations
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The mandates were an imperial arrangement made after the First World War, decades before the Cold War.

options.text: The partition of British India into India and Pakistan along religious lines at independence
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The 1947 partition came out of decolonization and religious politics, not a split between the Cold War blocs.

options.text: The division of Korea into rival states aligned with opposing sides in the Cold War
options.label: key
options.why: Like Germany and Berlin, Korea was divided after 1945 into a Soviet-backed communist state and a U.S.-backed state, with a fortified border between them.

facts: Korea was divided at the 38th parallel in 1945; separate northern and southern states were established in 1948.
The Korean War armistice of 1953 left a fortified demilitarized zone between North and South Korea.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line describes a city divided between an eastern and a western part, which invites comparison with other countries divided along Cold War lines.
design.evidence_quote: a wall dividing East Berlin from West Berlin

spec.theme: Economic planning and growth in India after independence

sources.context: This reference book was written for the U.S. government and describes India's economy after independence in 1947.

items.stem: The five-year plans that the excerpt credits to Jawaharlal Nehru are best explained as an example of which economic approach?

options.text: A mixed economy in which the state directed investment and owned key industries
options.label: key
options.why: Nehru's plans, starting in 1951, used central planning and public-sector heavy industry while still allowing a private sector. This fits the excerpt's goals of strong growth and higher incomes for the poor.

options.text: Forced collectivization of all farmland into state farms following the Soviet model under Stalin
options.label: overstated
options.why: Nehru borrowed the idea of planning from the Soviets, but India never forced all farmland into collectives. Indian agriculture stayed mostly in private hands.

options.text: Export-led growth built on low-wage manufacturing for American and European consumers
options.label: misattributed
options.why: This was the strategy of East Asian economies such as South Korea and Taiwan. Nehru's India stressed self-reliance and import substitution instead.

options.text: Free-market liberalization that cut tariffs, sold state firms, and invited foreign multinational investment
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This describes India's reforms that began in 1991, decades after Nehru, and it is the opposite of his state-led planning.

facts: India's First Five-Year Plan began in 1951 under Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru.
Nehru's India combined state-owned heavy industry with a private sector, an arrangement usually called a mixed economy.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt names Nehru as the leader who introduced the five-year plans and links them to growth and poverty-reduction goals.
design.evidence_quote: Jawaharlal Nehru, who introduced the five-year plans

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the authors' claim about the partition of British India?

options.text: Nehru and other leaders disagreed sharply about whether growth or poverty reduction came first
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt says India's leaders agreed that growth and higher incomes for the poor were both necessary goals.

options.text: Partition worsened economic problems that India had already inherited from colonial rule
options.label: key
options.why: The excerpt says that the problems inherited at independence were made worse by the costs of partition, including refugees and divided economic zones.

options.text: Refugee resettlement was a minor expense compared with the cost of building new heavy industry
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt calls refugee settlement a considerable financial strain and does not compare it with spending on industry.

options.text: Partition strengthened India's economy because West Bengal kept the jute and cotton fields of eastern Bengal
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt says the fields lay in eastern Bengal, which became East Pakistan. India kept the mills but lost the fields.

facts: The partition of British India in 1947 created India and Pakistan and set off one of the largest migrations in history.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The opening sentence states that partition made the inherited structural problems worse.
design.evidence_quote: the structural economic problems inherited at independence were exacerbated by the costs associated with the partition of British India

items.stem: The refugee movement across the new India-Pakistan borders described in the excerpt is best understood in the context of which broader process?

options.text: Cold War proxy conflicts in which the United States and Soviet Union armed rival Indian states
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Partition came from the end of British rule and from communal divisions, not from superpower proxy wars between Indian states.

options.text: Rural-to-urban migration caused by Green Revolution mechanization of farming in Punjab
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Green Revolution began in the mid-1960s, long after the refugee movements of 1947.

options.text: Post-1945 decolonization that drew new borders along religious or ethnic lines
options.label: key
options.why: Britain withdrew from South Asia in 1947 and partitioned it largely along Hindu-Muslim lines. Millions were displaced. Decolonization produced similar partition crises elsewhere, such as Palestine in 1948.

options.text: Late nineteenth-century migration of indentured South Asian laborers to plantations in the Caribbean and Africa
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Indentured labor migration was a feature of nineteenth-century imperialism, not of the 1947 independence settlement.

facts: Britain partitioned British India into India and Pakistan at independence in 1947.
Partition displaced roughly 12 to 14 million people, mostly Hindus and Sikhs moving to India and Muslims moving to Pakistan.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt describes millions of refugees fleeing across the new borders created when British India was partitioned at independence.
design.evidence_quote: about 12 million to 14 million refugees fleeing past each other across the new borders between India and Pakistan

items.stem: India's use of former food-producing land to grow jute and cotton after 1947, as described in the excerpt, most directly relates to which later development in India?

options.text: The 1971 war that created Bangladesh after East Pakistan broke away from West Pakistan
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The excerpt mentions Bangladesh, but the 1971 war came from political conflict inside Pakistan, not from India's agricultural choices.

options.text: Gandhi's Salt March of 1930, which protested British taxes on a basic necessity
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Salt March came before independence, so it cannot be a later result of land-use changes after 1947.

options.text: The 1991 liberalization reforms that dismantled the License Raj and welcomed foreign capital investment
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Liberalization was a response to a balance-of-payments crisis and to slow growth under planning. It was not a response to food scarcity caused by land use.

options.text: Adoption of Green Revolution high-yield seeds in the 1960s to raise food output
options.label: key
options.why: Pressure on food supplies, which the land shift made worse, led to food shortages in the mid-1960s. India responded by adopting high-yield wheat and rice, fertilizers, and irrigation.

facts: India faced serious food shortages in the mid-1960s.
India adopted Green Revolution high-yield seed varieties beginning in the mid-1960s, especially in Punjab.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt says India had to turn food-producing land over to cash crops for its mills, which reduced the land available for food.
design.evidence_quote: India had to employ land previously used for food production to cultivate cotton and jute for its mills

items.stem: The context line says this study was written for the U.S. government in 1995. Which situation in India at that time best explains U.S. interest in India's economic history?

options.text: India had begun liberalizing its economy in 1991, raising U.S. interest in trade
options.label: key
options.why: The 1991 reforms opened India to foreign trade and investment. This made background on India's economy useful to U.S. officials in the mid-1990s.

options.text: Britain had just granted India independence, so U.S. diplomats needed new information
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Independence came in 1947, nearly fifty years before the study was written.

options.text: India had just founded the Non-Aligned Movement, rejecting alliance with either superpower
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Non-Aligned Movement was founded in 1961, and the Cold War had ended by 1995.

options.text: India had recently adopted Soviet-style central planning for the first time under Indira Gandhi
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Planning began under Nehru in 1951, as the excerpt notes. By 1995 India was moving away from planning, not taking it up.

facts: India began major economic liberalization reforms in 1991.
The Non-Aligned Movement was founded in 1961.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The credit line dates the study to 1995 and the context line says it was written for the U.S. government. That timing places it shortly after India's 1991 reforms.

items.stem: The five-year plans introduced by Nehru, as mentioned in the excerpt, were most similar to which development in another country?

options.text: Chile's free-market reforms under Pinochet, guided by economists trained in Chicago
options.label: reversal
options.why: Chile's reforms in the 1970s and 1980s were neoliberal and market-driven, not centrally planned.

options.text: China's First Five-Year Plan of 1953, which funded heavy industry
options.label: key
options.why: Like Nehru's plans, China's 1953 plan used state planning to direct investment into heavy industry. Both drew on the Soviet model.

options.text: Reagan's tax cuts and deregulation, which reduced the government's role in the U.S. economy
options.label: reversal
options.why: Reagan's policies in the 1980s shrank the state's economic role, which is the opposite of state-led planning.

options.text: Deng Xiaoping's special economic zones, which drew foreign investment to coastal China
options.label: reversal
options.why: Deng's zones, begun around 1980, moved China toward market forces and foreign capital, away from planned growth.

facts: China launched its First Five-Year Plan in 1953 with Soviet assistance, emphasizing heavy industry.
Deng Xiaoping created special economic zones beginning around 1980.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt names five-year plans as Nehru's main tool for reaching national economic growth goals.
design.evidence_quote: who introduced the five-year plans
